Florida homestead also has devise limits that matter when an owner dies.

Does Florida use a transfer on death deed?

Florida homeowners who want a house to skip probate generally use an enhanced life estate deed, commonly called a lady bird deed. Before using any form labeled a TOD deed that you find online, ask a Florida real property attorney whether the statutes authorize it.

The practical goal is the same in either case: the owner keeps control during life and the house passes to named people at death. This page explains the lady bird version, the homestead rule that limits it and the tax and title points a buyer or heir will meet.

What is a lady bird deed in Florida?

It is a deed in which the owner keeps a life estate with extra powers, and the remainder passes to named beneficiaries. A letter in the Florida Bar Journal describes the arrangement: the owner may sell, lease or otherwise transfer the property without the remainder persons' consent, and absent such a sale, title passes to them at death once a death certificate is filed in the official records.

The author of that letter also notes that in his office such a deed costs about the same as a simple will, and that it suits families whose main asset is the home and whose heirs could not easily pay for a probate.

Is a lady bird deed subject to documentary stamp tax?

On the facts reviewed in one Department of Revenue advisement, no. Technical Assistance Advisement 20B4-004, dated October 16, 2020, says the deed in question did not transfer any present beneficial interest, so it was not subject to documentary stamp tax whatever consideration was stated (TAA 20B4-004). The life tenants in that case kept full powers.

An advisement answers a specific set of facts, so a family should confirm treatment with the clerk's office or the attorney drafting the deed. Compare that result with the general rule on the Department's documentary stamp page: quit claim and life estate deeds are listed as taxable, and the page states there is no specific exemption for estate planning transfers of Florida real property.

Why does Florida homestead complicate a deed at death?

Florida limits what an owner can leave by will or trust. Under section 732.4015, homestead cannot be devised when the owner leaves a spouse or a minor child, except that it may go to a spouse if there is no minor child.

The statute counts a trust disposition as a devise. Because of that, owners with a spouse or young children should speak to an attorney about whether the deed they plan will work as intended. A deed signed years earlier can behave differently from a will, and the attorney's answer depends on the family and the property.

How does a transfer of title affect Florida property taxes?

A change of ownership usually resets assessed value to just value the following January 1. The Department of Revenue's Save Our Homes guide explains that any sale, foreclosure or transfer of legal or beneficial title counts, with exceptions such as transfers between spouses and certain transfers at death (Save Our Homes guide).

  • Under section 193.155, a quitclaim is a change of ownership unless an exception applies, such as the same person remaining entitled, a spouse transfer or a correction.
  • Homestead status requires the owner's permanent residence and an application by March 1.
  • Heirs who do not live in the house do not qualify for homestead on it.

Ask the county property appraiser how a particular deed will affect next year's assessment.

What signing and recording rules apply to a Florida deed?

A conveyance of an interest in land needs a signed writing made in front of two subscribing witnesses. Section 689.01 adds that no seal is needed and that witnessing can happen by audio-video technology.

Recording takes place at the clerk's office. The statutory recording charge listed in section 28.24 is five dollars for page one and four dollars for each extra page, with a trust fund charge and a technology charge per page on top. Call the recording desk for the total on your deed, because page count drives it.

What does a lady bird deed mean when an heir wants to sell?

After the owner dies, the beneficiaries hold the property, and the title insurer will want to see the recorded instrument and a death certificate. Sometimes it asks for additional proof on liens or the owner's marital status.

Florida deed choices for passing a house at death
ToolKey point
Lady bird deedOwner keeps power to sell; passes at death
Will or trustHomestead limits for spouse and minor children
Quitclaim deedTaxable deed; change of ownership unless exception

Heirs planning a sale should check early that every beneficiary will sign the sale deed.

What risks come with using a lady bird deed?

The main risk is a gap between the family's plan and the facts. A deed may name beneficiaries who die first, and a beneficiary's own creditors or divorce may touch what that person is due to receive. The attorney should address each prior to recording.

Another risk is paper that sits unrecorded. A deed that never reaches the Official Records gives a buyer or a title insurer nothing to read. The Florida Bar letter describes passage of title at death by filing a death certificate in the official records, so the recording step carries real weight.

Families also forget that the deed controls only that house. Bank accounts, vehicles and other assets need their own beneficiary designations, and a will still matters for anything outside the deed. The same letter recommends pairing the deed with pay on death and beneficiary designations on financial accounts.

What should an owner ask an attorney before signing a lady bird deed?

Bring a list of questions, because the deed has effects beyond probate. Each one below ties to a rule on this page.

  • Does the deed fit my homestead situation if I have a spouse or minor child?
  • Will recording it reset the assessed value or affect my exemptions?
  • Which of my children or relatives will need to sign if I sell during my life?
  • What happens if a beneficiary dies before me, or if I want to change my mind?
  • Does my mortgage lender or title insurer need notice?

The Florida Bar letter above notes that the owner keeps the power to sell or transfer the property without the remainder persons' consent, which is the feature most families want. The attorney can also tell you how a deed interacts with a will already on file and with beneficiary designations on bank accounts.

Families sometimes find an old deed in a drawer and wonder whether it already did the job. Read the recorded version at the clerk's office, not a copy, since the recorded text controls.

Frequently asked questions

Is a TOD deed available to Florida owners?

Ask a Florida real property attorney. Florida owners commonly use an enhanced life estate deed, also called a lady bird deed, to pass a house at death.

Does a lady bird deed avoid probate?

It is designed to, by passing title to the beneficiaries at death once a death certificate is recorded. Your attorney can confirm that it fits your family and your homestead situation.

Does a lady bird deed pay doc stamp tax?

One Department of Revenue advisement from 2020 found no tax on the facts presented, because no present beneficial interest passed. Confirm your own deed with the clerk or attorney.

Can homestead be left to anyone?

No. With a surviving spouse or minor child, homestead cannot be devised, except to the spouse when there is no minor child, under section 732.4015.

How many witnesses does a Florida deed need?

Two subscribing witnesses, under section 689.01, and no seal. Witnessing can use audio-video technology.

Florida Lady Bird Deed: Enhanced Life Estate Deeds and Selling the Home

Last updated November 14, 2026.

A Florida enhanced life estate deed, usually called a lady bird deed, lets the grantor keep a life estate and control of the property while naming who receives it later. This guide uses a clerk-published form and the Florida Constitution's homestead rules.

Selling a house in Florida?
Get My Cash Offer →

What is a lady bird deed in Florida?

A lady bird deed is a deed that leaves the owner a life estate carrying extra powers and names the people who take afterward. It is also called an enhanced life estate deed, and the state revenue agency has written about its tax treatment in an advisement dated October 16, 2020.

Look first at the wording of the deed itself: which powers the owner keeps and who the named remainder people are. Two deeds that both get called lady bird deeds can read differently, so the recorded text controls. Read it line by line before you plan a sale.

Does a lady bird deed owe Florida documentary stamp tax?

In the state revenue agency's advisement TAA 20B4-004, the answer was no, on the facts presented. The department concluded the deed did not transfer any present beneficial interest and was not subject to documentary stamp tax regardless of any consideration.

Those facts mattered. The life tenants in that request kept full powers over the property. A deed that gives up some of those powers could be analyzed differently, and the advisement answered one taxpayer's set of facts. Ask the clerk of court or a Florida real estate attorney before you record, because the tax is paid at that office.

For contrast, the agency's general page puts life estate deeds on its taxable list. Only the advisement's reasoning, that no present beneficial interest moves, explains why an enhanced life estate deed can be treated differently from an ordinary one.

How does a lady bird deed affect selling the home?

A sale starts with a deed to the buyer signed with the formalities Florida requires, so the first question is who must sign.

Under section 689.01 a land conveyance has to be written, with two subscribing witnesses watching the signing. No seal is required, and the witnessing can happen over audio-video technology. Whether the named remainder people must also sign turns on the powers written into your deed. The title agent will read the recorded text before agreeing to insure, so put that question to the agent before you list.

  • Pull the recorded deed from the clerk's official records.
  • Check which powers the deed reserves to the owner, including selling and mortgaging.
  • Find out whether the underwriter will insure with only the owner signing.
  • Plan for the sale deed to be taxed at the standard doc stamp rate.

What does the deed do to the tax bill?

The tax effect depends on whether a transfer counts as a title change. Under section 193.155, a sale, foreclosure or other transfer of legal or beneficial title sends the assessment back to just value on the next New Year's Day. Spousal transfers and certain transfers at death are among the exceptions.

The state chart prints a 2026 cap of 2.7 percent, 2.9 percent for 2025 and 3.0 percent for 2024, a year when CPI ran 3.4 percent and the 3 percent ceiling governed. The advisement reasoned that nothing beneficial passes at signing. Whether the property appraiser's office reads your deed the same way is a separate question, and one to ask before leaning on that reading.

The homestead exemption runs up to $50,000, with the first $25,000 reaching school taxes and the second $25,000 hitting only non-school taxes on value above $50,000. Form DR-501 starts it. Renting the unit or moving out ends it.

Can the owner carry the tax cap to a replacement home?

Portability lets an owner move part of the Save Our Homes savings to a new Florida home. The new homestead must be set up within three years counted from the opening day of the calendar year the old one was abandoned, with the sale date playing no part in that count.

Form DR-501T goes in with the new DR-501 before the early-spring filing deadline. Section 193.155(8) reduces the new home's assessed value by the lesser of $500,000 or the gap between just value and assessed value on the old home. The statute page notes that amendments from chapter 2026-239 first apply to the 2027 tax roll, so ask the property appraiser which version applies to your filing year.

  • The old home's sale resets the buyer's assessment to just value.
  • Filing for homestead closes on March 1.
  • Residence must be in place on the assessment date, January 1.
  • Renting the home, moving out or leaving Florida ends the exemption.

How do common deed types compare for tax?

Deed type drives the tax result, who must sign and what the title insurer will accept, and each difference shows up at closing.

Deed typeDoc stamp result
Lady bird (enhanced life estate), on the facts in TAA 20B4-004Not subject, regardless of consideration
Life estate deedListed as a taxable deed
Quit claim deedListed as a taxable deed
Agreement or contract for deedListed as a taxable deed

Source: Florida Department of Revenue.

The state agency adds two rules for any taxable deed. Everyone named on the document is liable for the tax, and if one party is exempt a non-exempt party must pay. Deeds are taxable whether or not they are recorded. Recording costs follow section 28.24, which also adds a $1.00 charge for each name beyond four on an instrument.

What documents should a seller line up before listing?

Begin with the deed on record and the questions it raises: who holds the life estate, which powers are reserved, and who is named to receive the property later. Take those answers to the title agent, then to the closing attorney if anything is unclear.

  • Government photo identification for each person who will sign the sale deed.
  • The names of two adults who can witness the signing in person or by audio-video link.
  • A payoff statement for any mortgage on the property.
  • Your latest tax bill, to see if homestead is applied.

Each item shortens the time between a signed contract and a recorded deed, and a seller who arrives with them gives the title company fewer reasons to pause.

What if the owner wants to sell fast with a lady bird deed in place?

Cash buyers still want clean title. Gather the recorded deed, the legal description and any mortgage payoff before you talk to them.

The closing agent will verify each signer, pay off liens from proceeds and send the sale deed for recording with its tax. After an owner's death, the deed's own terms and any probate steps decide who signs next, and the underwriter will say which court papers it wants. Recording questions go to the clerk's office.

Frequently asked questions

Is a lady bird deed subject to Florida doc stamp tax?

Not on the facts in advisement TAA 20B4-004, dated October 16, 2020, where the life tenants kept full powers. The department said no present beneficial interest passed, so no tax applied regardless of consideration. Confirm your own facts with the clerk or an attorney.

Do I need two witnesses on a lady bird deed?

Yes. Florida's conveyance statute, section 689.01, calls for a written deed with two subscribing witnesses. A seal is optional, and audio-video witnessing is allowed.

May a life tenant list and sell the property?

Often yes, depending on the powers your deed reserves. Show the title company the recorded deed first. It will tell you whether your signature alone is enough or whether the named remainder people must join.

Does a lady bird deed keep my homestead exemption?

The exemption depends on the home staying your permanent residence, not on the deed type. Renting the home or moving out ends it, and a title change resets the Save Our Homes assessment. Ask the county property appraiser how your deed is classified.

Which office records a lady bird deed?

File it at the circuit court clerk's office serving the land's county. Any documentary stamp tax is collected there at recording, along with the page fees in section 28.24.

Florida Squatters Rights: Adverse Possession and the Sheriff Removal Process

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Florida requires 7 years of actual continued possession under a claim of title for adverse possession without color of title, and an owner can ask the county sheriff for removal of people unlawfully occupying a home under Sec. 82.036.

Selling a house in Florida?
Get My Cash Offer →

Do squatters have rights to a house in Florida?

Only in a narrow case: a person can eventually claim title by adverse possession, but the statute demands seven years of possession plus paid property taxes, and unlawful occupants face removal long before that. For an owner of a Florida house, the faster tool is the sheriff removal process in section 82.036.

This page walks through both rules so an owner can see why a squatter's claim is weak and how to regain possession. A tenant is different from a squatter, and a lease changes which law applies.

How does adverse possession work without a deed?

Under section 95.18, a claimant needs seven years of actual, continued possession under a claim of title that is not based on a written instrument. The claimant must also meet tax conditions.

  • Pay all outstanding taxes within one year of entering the property.
  • File a return with the county property appraiser within 30 days after that payment.
  • Keep paying taxes for every year of the claim.

Possession counts when the land is protected by a substantial enclosure or cultivated, maintained or improved in a usual manner. The property appraiser mails the return to the record owner and notes the claim on the tax roll, which gives the owner written warning.

What changes when the claimant holds a written instrument?

Adverse possession under color of title also runs seven years, but it starts from a written conveyance, decree or judgment. Section 95.16 requires that, for possession that began after December 31, 1945, the instrument be recorded with the clerk of the circuit court in the county where the land lies.

The statute lists what counts as possession: usual cultivation or improvement, a substantial enclosure, use for fuel or fencing timber, or partial improvement of a known lot or single farm. Where land is enclosed, only the part included in the written description is treated as possessed.

Is living in a house on an adverse possession claim legal in Florida?

Not before the claimant files the return. Section 95.18 says that occupying a residential structure solely on an adverse possession claim before the return is filed is trespass under section 810.08, and offering the home for lease is theft under section 812.014.

This matters for owners, because a person who moves into a vacant house and says they have rights has not started a legitimate clock. A police report and a sheriff complaint are the owner's next steps. Do not change the locks on someone who holds a lease or has received mail there for months without asking an attorney, because the removal statute only fits a narrow set of facts.

How does the sheriff removal process work in Florida?

The owner or the owner's agent files a verified Complaint to Remove Persons Unlawfully Occupying Residential Real Property with the sheriff. Section 82.036 sets the conditions, and the sheriff then serves a notice to vacate immediately and puts the owner back in possession.

The statute lists these requirements:

  • The property is residential and not open to the public.
  • No tenancy exists and the occupants are not family of the owner.
  • The owner has told the occupants to leave.
  • No litigation about the property is pending.

A false statement carries a price. The occupant can recover damages, including statutory damages of triple the fair market rent, plus costs and attorney fees. Treat the complaint like a sworn court filing.

What if the occupant is a tenant or a former tenant?

Then Florida's landlord and tenant chapter governs, not the squatter statute. For unpaid rent, section 83.56 calls for three days' written notice, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and court-observed holidays, demanding rent or possession.

A tenant who raises a defense other than payment must put the accrued rent into the court registry within five days, again excluding weekends and holidays, or the landlord can obtain a default judgment (section 83.60). After judgment the clerk issues a writ and the sheriff gives 24 hours' posted notice before restoring possession (section 83.62).

What should an owner document before asking the sheriff to act?

Keep proof that you own the house and that nobody ever had your permission to stay. A recorded deed and a current property tax bill usually answer the first point, and a written demand to leave answers the second.

  • Photos or video of the occupied home with dates.
  • Any message in which you told the occupants to leave.
  • Confirmation that no lease, rent payment or family tie exists.
  • A search of the county court records for any pending case about the house.

Each item lines up with a condition printed in section 82.036, so the sworn complaint can state the facts without guessing. If a court case about the property is open, the sheriff route is unavailable and the attorney handling that case is the person to call.

How does a squatter claim affect a sale or the property tax roll?

A return filed with the property appraiser leaves a mark on the tax roll, and buyers and title companies look at the roll and at the official records. An owner who learns of a filing should tell the closing attorney the same day, because the claim has to be answered before title can be called clean.

Paying the property tax bill on time on a vacant Florida house also takes away part of a claimant's story, since the adverse possession statute rests on the claimant paying the taxes. Owners of empty houses can ask the county property appraiser how to receive notice if a return arrives, and can check the tax collector's records for payments made by someone else.

Vacant houses invite trouble most often in the months after an owner dies or moves. A neighbor, a caretaker or a family member visiting weekly can spot a stranger early. An early report to the sheriff is easier to handle than a long occupancy.

SituationPathStatute

Claimant paying taxes and filing a returnCourt action over title95.18
Claimant with a recorded written instrumentCourt action over title95.16

If you cannot tell which row fits, ask a Florida real estate attorney or the sheriff's civil process unit before serving anything.

How can I sell a Florida house that has an unwanted occupant?

Resolve who has the right to be there first, since an occupant with a claim can complicate title and a closing. Owners often combine the sheriff or court step with a sale to a buyer who purchases as is.

Gather the deed, the latest tax bill, any notices you served and any police report. If the occupant files a property appraiser return, tell your attorney and the title company right away, because the claim appears on the tax roll.

Frequently asked questions

How long does adverse possession take in Florida?

Seven years of actual continued possession. The claimant also has to pay taxes and file a return with the property appraiser, so seven years of simply living there does not meet the statute.

Can I call the sheriff on squatters in my Florida home?

Yes, if the facts fit section 82.036: residential property, no tenancy, not family, you told them to leave, and no pending litigation. You submit a verified complaint and the sheriff serves the notice.

What if I lie on the sheriff complaint?

The occupant can seek damages, including statutory damages of triple the fair market rent, costs and attorney fees. File only with accurate facts.

Is a tenant who stopped paying a squatter?

No. A tenant falls under the landlord and tenant chapter, which starts with written notice and a court case. The sheriff acts after a judgment and a writ.

Does the claimant have to record anything?

Under color of title, the written instrument must be recorded with the circuit court clerk. Without color of title, the claimant files a return with the county property appraiser.

A Florida landlord can end a tenancy for unpaid rent with a written 3-day notice that excludes weekends and legal holidays, and must go to county court to recover possession. Landlords cannot lock tenants out. This guide summarizes Chapter 83 as the Florida Statutes show it.

Selling a house in Florida?

What are the steps in a Florida eviction?

A Florida eviction runs in five stages: written notice, a court complaint, the tenant's response, a judgment, and removal by the sheriff. Each stage has its own clock under Chapter 83 of the Florida Statutes.

The process only works in order. A landlord who changes the locks, shuts off the water or carries out the tenant's belongings has skipped the court stage, and that shortcut can bring its own claims. The slow, documented path is the one that ends with a writ in hand.

Owners who plan to sell also have to think about timing. Every stage adds days, and a buyer will want a close date that the court calendar can support.

What does the landlord have to do before going to court?

The landlord first serves a written notice that fits the problem. For unpaid rent that is a three day notice, excluding Saturdays, Sundays and court observed legal holidays, under section 83.56(3).

  • Lease breaches the tenant can fix: seven days to cure after delivery.
  • Breaches that cannot be fixed: seven days to vacate.
  • Same breach again within 12 months: suit may go ahead without a new notice.

The notice may be mailed, handed over, emailed under section 83.505 where that applies, or left at the home when the tenant is away. The lease cannot waive any of this. Our separate page on Florida eviction notices walks through each notice type in more detail.

What does the tenant have to do after being served?

A tenant who wants to fight on any ground other than payment must act fast. Within five days of service, again excluding Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays, the tenant must deposit the accrued rent into the court registry or ask the court to set the rent. Section 83.60(2) spells this out.

Missing that deadline waives every defense except payment, and the landlord can ask for an immediate default judgment. This is the point where many cases end, because a tenant who cannot post the money loses the chance to argue.

The deposit is not a penalty. It keeps the rent available to the landlord while the court decides. A tenant who has paid in full has a defense that does not need the deposit, and should bring proof of payment to the hearing.

What if the landlord takes partial rent during the case?

Taking some rent after serving the three day notice does not end the case, but it has rules. Under section 83.56, the landlord must hand the tenant a receipt that states the balance still due, pay the partial rent into the court registry when filing the complaint, or serve a new three day notice.

Landlords who ignore this and just cash the check hand the tenant an argument that the notice was waived. If you are not sure which path to take, ask the clerk of the county court where you plan to file, or consult a Florida attorney before accepting any money.

Tenants should also keep proof of every payment. A receipt, bank record or money order stub can settle a dispute about what was paid and when.

How does the judgment turn into a removal?

Once the court rules for the landlord, the clerk issues a writ of possession to the sheriff. The sheriff posts a notice at the home, and after 24 hours puts the landlord in possession. Weekends and holidays do not stay that 24 hour period, according to section 83.62.

Only the sheriff executes the writ. A landlord who is tempted to move things along by showing up with a moving crew is outside the statute. Keep the writ, the posting date and the date of possession in the file, since a title company may ask for them.

How do periodic tenancies fit into the process?

Not every removal needs a default. When a tenancy has no set end date, the landlord can end it by giving advance notice instead of proving a breach. Section 83.57 sets the length by rental period: not less than 30 days for month to month and quarter to quarter, 60 days for year to year, and 7 days for week to week.

The notice must come before the end of the period. If the tenant stays past the end date, the landlord then files in court and the usual stages apply, from the tenant's response through judgment and the sheriff's writ.

For an owner who wants to sell a house with no one inside, this is often the cleanest route, because it does not depend on a payment or lease problem. The cost is waiting out the notice period.

What documents does the owner need to keep?

  • The lease and any renewals or amendments.
  • The notice as served and the proof of how it was delivered.
  • A ledger of rent charged and received.
  • The court complaint, the tenant's answer, and any registry deposit record.
  • The judgment, writ of possession and sheriff's posting date.

A buyer's lender or title agent may ask for these papers when a rental sale follows an eviction. Keeping them in one folder saves time at closing.

Which timelines apply at a glance?

Curable breach notice7 days to cure83.56
Incurable breach notice7 days to vacate83.56

Can a landlord sell a rental house while an eviction is pending?

An owner may market a property that has an eviction in progress, but a buyer who closes with an occupant still inside inherits the problem. Most buyers financing a purchase will ask for vacant possession, so an unfinished case tends to push the close date out.

The practical options for an owner are:

  • Finish the eviction, then list the home with the keys in hand.
  • Offer the home to an investor who buys with the tenant in place.
  • Where the tenancy has no end date and the tenant is not in default, use the notice periods in section 83.57 and time the sale to the end of the period.

A Florida attorney or the clerk of the county court can confirm the local filing steps and fees. Rules and forms vary a little by county, so ask the clerk where you file.

What can go wrong in the process?

Most failed evictions come down to defects early on. The notice has the wrong number of days, it was never delivered the way the statute allows, or the landlord took partial rent after serving it without following the receipt, registry or new notice rule in section 83.56.

A second trouble spot is self help. Changing locks or removing a tenant's property outside the writ turns a landlord who was in the right into a defendant. The better habit is to keep every date, copy and receipt, and to let the sheriff carry out the final step.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a Florida eviction take?

The statutes set short clocks, 3 or 7 days for notices, 5 days for the tenant's deposit and 24 hours for the sheriff's posting. Court scheduling decides the rest, so ask the clerk of the county court for local timing.

Does the tenant have to pay money into the court?

Yes, if the tenant raises any defense other than payment. The accrued rent goes into the court registry, or a motion to determine rent is filed, within 5 days after service, excluding weekends and legal holidays.

Who carries out the eviction in Florida?

The sheriff does. After judgment the clerk issues a writ, and the sheriff posts a 24 hour notice before putting the landlord back in possession.

Can I accept part of the rent after serving the notice?

Only with care. The landlord must give a receipt showing the balance, pay the partial amount into the court registry when filing, or serve a new three day notice.

Can I sell the house with a tenant still living in it?

Yes, but the buyer takes the situation as it stands. Closing is usually faster once the tenancy has ended or a buyer agrees to take the home occupied.

Florida summary administration is available when the estate subject to administration is within the statutory limit or the decedent has been dead more than 2 years. The statute currently shows a $150,000 limit after a 2026 amendment, not the older $75,000 figure.

What is summary administration in Florida?

Summary administration is the shortened court process Florida offers for a small or old estate, and it can clear title to an inherited house without a full probate. The rules sit in chapter 735 of the Florida Statutes, in the part titled Probate Code: Small Estates.

The court enters one order that assigns the estate to the people entitled to it. That order is what a title company reads when a beneficiary wants to sell the house. If you inherited a Florida home and the paperwork feels heavy, this route is worth a conversation with a probate attorney before anything is listed.

Does my Florida estate qualify for summary administration?

It qualifies if the estate has a value of $150,000 or less after exempt property is set aside, or if the person has been dead for more than two years. The limit comes from section 735.201, whose page history lists a 2026 amendment (chapter 2026-57), so check the current text with the clerk or an attorney before relying on an older figure such as $75,000.

  • The decedent may be a Florida resident or a nonresident with Florida assets.
  • Exempt property under the Florida Constitution and statutes is left out of the value count.
  • A will can block the route if it directs administration as chapter 733 requires.

A house is often the largest asset, so the size test depends on whether the home counts as exempt homestead. That question turns on the facts, which is why the court and the clerk matter more than any online estimate.

Who files the petition and who has to sign?

Any beneficiary, or the person a will nominates as personal representative, can file the petition. Under section 735.203, the surviving spouse and the beneficiaries must sign and verify it.

A beneficiary who receives a full share under the proposed distribution does not have to join. That person still receives formal notice. When a signer has died, is a minor, or lacks capacity, a representative or guardian signs instead, and a person who bought a beneficiary's interest may sign in that beneficiary's place. For a family spread across several states, this signature requirement is usually the slowest part.

What does the court order do for a buyer of the house?

The order allows immediate distribution and, under section 735.206, protects a purchaser. Someone who pays value to a person assigned the property takes it free of the decedent's creditors and of the claims of a spouse and other beneficiaries.

That protection is why a title insurer will usually accept the order as the link in the chain of title. The statute also sets limits you should know about:

  • Before the order, the petitioner must search for known or reasonably findable creditors, serve them with the petition and provide for payment as far as assets allow.
  • Heirs who receive property are personally liable for a pro rata share of lawful claims, up to the value they actually received.
  • After two years from the death, the estate and its recipients are no longer liable for claims unless proceedings to enforce them began.
  • An heir left out of the order can pursue the people who obtained it and may recover attorney fees.

Which Florida estates need no administration at all?

An estate needs none when it holds only exempt personal property plus a small amount of other personal property. Section 735.301 sets the ceiling for the non-exempt part at preferred funeral expenses and reasonable medical and hospital costs from the last 60 days of the final illness.

The court may then authorize a transfer on an informal application. A house does not fit this track in most cases, because real estate is neither exempt personal property nor small in value. Treat this section as relevant to bank accounts and vehicles, and use summary administration or formal administration for land.

How do creditor deadlines affect selling an inherited Florida home?

Creditors lose their claims once the filing deadline passes, which makes the deadline a practical date for heirs. Under section 733.702, a claim is barred unless filed by the later of three months after first publication of the notice to creditors or 30 days after service on a creditor who had to be served.

Summary administration runs on its own two year outer limit, described above. Ask the probate attorney which clock applies to your file, since publication dates and service dates vary by case.

Does Florida charge estate tax or deed tax on an inherited house?

Florida levies no estate tax for deaths after December 31, 2004. Since July 1, 2023, personal representatives skip Forms DR-312 and DR-313, per the revenue agency estate tax page. Federal rules are separate.

Documentary stamp tax is the cost that surprises heirs. The agency's stamp tax page lists a personal representative's deed under a probated will as not taxable, yet states that estate planning transfers of Florida real property have no specific exemption. When the heirs later deed the house to a buyer, that deed is taxable in the ordinary way, and the rate per $100 differs in Miami-Dade, so read the page for your county.

What does the homestead rule do to a will in Florida?

Florida homestead cannot be left by will when the owner is survived by a spouse or a minor child, with one exception: it may go to a spouse when no minor child exists. That is section 732.4015, and it treats a trust disposition the same way as a devise.

So a will that names a sibling as heir to the family home may not control who inherits it. Before anyone signs a sale contract, a probate attorney should confirm who actually holds title, because a buyer needs the right signatures on the deed.

Which steps and records come first before a sale?

Collect the death certificate, the will if there is one, the deed to the house and the latest tax bill. Then compare the estate with the statute above and decide between summary and formal administration.

What is the Florida summary administration limit?

The limit is $150,000 in non-exempt value, or the decedent having been dead more than two years. Section 735.201 shows a 2026 amendment, so confirm the current figure with the clerk of the court.

Is it possible to sell an inherited Florida house before the court order?

Usually not, because the heirs need an order or other proof of who holds title. A buyer's title company decides what it will accept, so ask it early and ask the probate attorney who must sign.

Do all heirs have to sign the petition?

Most do. The surviving spouse and the beneficiaries sign, except a beneficiary receiving a full distributive share, who is not required to join but must receive formal notice.

Will creditors still be able to collect after summary administration?

Yes, for a limited time. Heirs share liability for lawful claims up to what they received, and the exposure ends two years after death unless enforcement proceedings began.

Does Florida have an estate tax on a house passing to heirs?

No. Florida has no estate tax for deaths after 2004. Doc stamp tax can still apply to deeds, so ask the clerk or an attorney how your deed is treated.

Does Florida levy an inheritance or estate tax?

No. The revenue agency explains that a federal change ended Florida's estate tax for anyone dying after December 31, 2004, and since July 1, 2023 personal representatives skip Forms DR-312 and DR-313 (estate tax page).

Receiving a Florida house therefore triggers no state tax on its own. If a lender, buyer or relative asks, point them to that page.

Three other charges can still matter: federal estate tax on very large estates, federal tax on gain, and stamp tax on a deed that moves title for value.

When does federal estate tax reach a Florida estate?

Only above a high filing line. The IRS requires a return when the decedent's gross estate, plus lifetime taxable gifts and the gift tax exemption used, tops the threshold for the death year (IRS estate tax).

Year of deathFiling threshold
2025$13,990,000

Source: IRS estate tax page. Deductions cover debts, administration costs and property passing to a surviving spouse or qualified charity, and spouses can carry over unused exemption by filing on time.

What is an heir's basis when selling an inherited Florida house?

Usually the property's value on the day of death, not the decedent's purchase price. Publication 551 also permits a later valuation date if the personal representative chooses one (Pub. 551).

When an estate files Form 706, the executor generally sends beneficiaries a Schedule A (Form 8971) showing the reported value, and some must adopt it as their starting basis. Without one, the appraised value used for state inheritance or transmission tax can serve.

One exception exists: appreciated property that you or your spouse gave the decedent within a year before death keeps the decedent's adjusted basis.

Keep any appraisal made around the death in the estate file, and let a CPA relate it to your sale price.

Who reports income from selling an inherited house?

The heir does, on a federal return. A sale near the stepped-up value tends to leave little gain, while a sale well above it can leave more. A CPA can say whether any other return applies to you.

How is a deed taxed when an inherited house changes hands?

The route matters. The revenue agency treats the deed a personal representative signs under a probated will as untaxed, while warranty, special warranty, quit claim and life estate deeds are on its taxable list (doc stamp page).

A taxable deed pays 70 cents on every $100 of consideration outside Miami-Dade, and consideration counts any mortgage or encumbrance, assumed or not. The agency adds that no exemption exists just because a transfer is estate planning. A gift of a mortgaged house can therefore be taxed even with no cash exchanged (s. 201.02).

  • Probated will: the deed signed by the representative is the untaxed route.
  • Quitclaim between heirs: taxable if debt attaches.
  • Every party to a taxable deed is liable, whoever agrees to pay.

Which probate rules set the pace for heirs who want to sell?

Three statutes frame the timeline. Summary administration fits an estate with non-exempt assets up to $150,000, or a death more than two years ago (s. 735.201). A creditor must file by the later of three months after the first publication of notice or 30 days after being served, if service was required (s. 733.702). Where only exempt or tiny personal property remains, a court can allow transfer without administration (s. 735.301).

Homestead adds a layer. With a spouse or minor child surviving, the homestead cannot be devised, so a will may not decide title, and a spouse has six months to elect a half interest instead of a life estate (s. 732.401). Learn what the title insurer wants before you list.

Property tax keeps accruing while the estate is open. Transfer at death can reset just value the next January 1 unless an exception applies.

How do property taxes behave after the owner dies?

They keep running. Assessment is fixed each January 1, and the tax collector sends bills in November with discounts of 4 percent, 3, 2 and 1 across November through February (state calendar). An heir cannot skip them because the estate is open.

The homestead exemption depends on permanent residence, and the department's guide says it ends once the home is no longer the owner's permanent home. After a death the estate or heir should ask the appraiser how to treat the parcel on the next roll.

Change of ownership rules matter as well. A transfer of title resets the parcel to just value the next January 1, though the state names spousal transfers and certain transfers at death as exceptions (assessment guide). A buyer from the estate will usually see a reset.

Can heirs spread out a tax bill on an inherited house?

Sometimes. Installment prepayment requires an application to the tax collector by May 1 of the assessment year (s. 197.222), and partial payments before the delinquency date are left to the collector's discretion (s. 197.374). A homestead deferral through Form DR-570 is due by March 31 after the assessment year and depends on household income.

Those options turn on who lives in the home, since homestead status requires permanent residence. If the heir does not live there, ask the tax collector which plan, if any, fits a non-homestead parcel, and pay before April 1 to avoid delinquency (state calendar).

Ask for written confirmation of any arrangement and keep it with the estate records, so the closing agent can show the buyer that no balance is left behind.

What paperwork should heirs have ready for the sale?

  • A date-of-death appraisal or a Schedule A, if issued, to document basis.
  • Letters or a summary administration order showing who may sign.
  • A recorded spousal election, if one was made on homestead.
  • The newest tax bill and any deferral papers.
  • The reasoning for how each deed is taxed or exempt under chapter 201.

No Florida estate tax return exists to chase, and Form 706 matters only above the IRS line for the year of death.

If heirs disagree on price or buyer, the court may have to decide. Raise that early, because an empty house still produces tax, insurance and upkeep costs.

How should heirs weigh selling quickly against holding the house?

Holding costs decide most cases. The state tax bill arrives every November, delinquency starts April 1, and a vacant house still needs insurance, utilities and repairs. Against that, a sale at a price near the day-of-death value usually leaves little gain to report.

Heirs sometimes assume a probate delay changes the tax picture. It does not remove the November bill, and it does not postpone the reset in assessed value that follows a transfer of title. Compare the monthly carrying cost with the likely sale price, and ask a CPA or attorney how your own facts fit before you commit to a buyer.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a Florida inheritance tax?

No. Estate tax ended for deaths after December 31, 2004, and the state lists no inheritance levy. Receiving a house creates no state tax by itself.

When would federal estate tax apply to a house I inherit?

Only if the estate exceeds the IRS filing line, set at $15,000,000 for a 2026 death. The estate files and pays, and most estates fall below the line.

What basis do I use on an inherited Florida house?

Generally its worth on the day of death, or a later valuation date if the estate chose that route. A Schedule A (Form 8971) reports the figure when an estate return was filed.

Is a personal representative's deed taxed?

The revenue agency lists it as untaxed when it follows a probated will. Quit claim and warranty deeds are taxable, at the 70 cent rate used outside Miami-Dade.

Who reports gain on an inherited house sale?

You do, on your federal return. A stepped-up basis typically keeps gain small on a prompt sale, and a CPA can confirm.

A Florida deed must be signed in the presence of two subscribing witnesses (Sec. 689.01), and the clerk will record it only if it carries printed names and post-office addresses. Documentary stamp tax on deeds is 70 cents per $100 of consideration.

What does a Florida warranty deed do?

A Florida warranty deed moves title to land and carries the grantor's promise that the title is good. The statutory form says the grantor "does hereby fully warrant the title to said land, and will defend the same against the lawful claims of all persons whomsoever."

That promise is the difference between a warranty deed and a quit claim deed, which hands over whatever interest the grantor holds without vouching for it. Buyers who pay full price, and their lenders, usually expect the stronger form. Section 689.02 sets out the sample wording, and a deed may be built on it.

What must a warranty deed contain to be valid and recordable?

Section 689.01 asks for a signed writing with two subscribing witnesses present. A seal is optional, and witnesses may appear by audio-video link.

Getting the deed onto the public record takes more. Section 695.26 bars the clerk from filing the paper unless it shows:

  • Each signer's name printed beneath the signature, with a post-office address.
  • Whoever drafted it, named as a real person with a mailing address.
  • Each witness's name printed beneath the signature, with an address.
  • The name of the notary or other officer taking the acknowledgment, printed under that signature.
  • Empty corner room at upper right, larger on page one, reserved for clerk stamps.
  • Every buyer's name and address, written out.

Out-of-state signings, court orders and wills are carved out of that section. If a clerk accepts a deed that misses a step, the statute says the recording and its constructive notice still stand.

Is a parcel number required on a Florida deed?

The statutory form includes a blank for the property appraiser's parcel identification number, but a missing or wrong number does not void the deed.

Section 689.02(2) says the number, when available, should be entered before recording. It is not part of the legal description and cannot replace it. Copy the legal description exactly from the prior deed or a survey, then add the parcel number as a convenience for the clerk and the appraiser.

What stamp tax applies to a Florida deed?

The statute sets the deed rate at 70 cents for each $100 of consideration. Miami-Dade runs on a different schedule: 60 cents, plus a 45 cent surtax that skips a document moving only a single-family home.

The statute reads consideration widely: cash, a released debt, and any loan secured on the land, assumed or not. A deed reciting a token sum can therefore still draw tax on the mortgage balance.

Responsibility is shared. The revenue department says every party answers for the tax whatever the contract says, and an exempt party's share shifts to a non-exempt one. Unrecorded deeds are not outside the tax.

Which transfers escape the deed tax, and which do not?

Few transfers escape, and the revenue department names no exemption aimed at estate planning.

Deed types and documentary stamp tax, as listed by the Department of Revenue
DocumentTaxable?
Warranty, special warranty, quit claim, trustee and life estate deedsListed as taxable
Deed in lieu of foreclosure, contract for deed, certificate of titleListed as taxable
Deed from a personal representative acting under a probated willListed as not taxable
Spouse-to-spouse homestead deed backed only by a mortgage; marital home deed in a divorceExempt under s. 201.02(7)

Lady bird deeds get separate handling. In an October 2020 advisement, the revenue department treated one, where the life tenants kept full powers, as passing no present beneficial interest and so outside stamp tax. Whether your deed fits that fact pattern is a question for a Florida attorney.

What are the clerk's recording charges?

Section 28.24(13) fixes these fees, which come on top of stamp tax.

  • Page one costs $5.00 and each later page $4.00 (standard size, up to 14 by 8.5 inches).
  • An extra $1.00 per name after the fourth.
  • A records modernization trust fund fee: $1.00 for page one, $0.50 afterward.
  • An additional $4 per page technology charge.

Ask the clerk's office for the total for your page count.

What other stamp taxes can appear around a sale?

Mortgage paperwork is taxed separately from the deed. The Department of Revenue prints 35 cents per $100 of the amount secured for mortgages and notes, with the tax on a note capped at $2,450 and no cap on mortgages.

After a foreclosure sale, the certificate of title is taxed on the best bid made (s. 201.02(9)). For an ordinary sale between private parties, expect the deed tax to be the main figure, and ask your closing agent whether the buyer's new loan adds its own charges.

How should a seller prepare a deed before closing?

Assemble the pieces early, because a clerk can reject an instrument at the counter and the closing then slips.

  • Pull the legal description from your vesting deed and copy it character for character.
  • Confirm the exact way each grantor's name appears in the record, and use the same spelling.
  • Line up two adult witnesses and a notary on the signing day, or ask the title company about remote witnessing.
  • Print every name and mailing address where the statute wants it.
  • Leave the top right corner of each page clear for the clerk.

Then confirm with the closing agent what stamp tax will be due and who funds it.

Which deed fits a sale and which fits a family transfer?

For an arm's-length sale at market price, buyers and lenders generally look for a warranty deed, since it carries the title promise. A quit claim deed passes only what the grantor owns and is common between relatives or to fix a name on the record, though the revenue department still lists it among taxable deeds.

An agreement or contract for deed is listed as taxable too, and the buyer under a recorded contract for deed is one of the people notified before a tax deed sale. Section 689.01 reaches any conveyance of a freehold or of a term longer than one year, so a long lease needs the same two witnesses.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

How does a deed affect property taxes after the sale?

Title passing by sale, foreclosure or any other route counts as a change of ownership for assessment. Just value applies from the next January 1, and the seller's Save Our Homes cap stays behind.

Spousal transfers and some transfers at death are carved out. A quitclaim to a relative is not an exception just because no money changes hands. Buyers should file for their own homestead exemption with the county property appraiser by March 1, and should look into portability if they held a homestead elsewhere in the state.

Frequently asked questions

Do both spouses have to sign a Florida warranty deed?

Not always, but a married owner should confirm whether the home is homestead before signing. Homestead rules on spousal joinder sit outside the statutes reviewed here, so ask a Florida title attorney or title company. Any signer must still follow the two-witness and printed-name rules.

Can I use a warranty deed to give a house to my child?

Yes, but the transfer is a change of ownership for assessment purposes and can carry stamp tax on any mortgage balance. The Department of Revenue lists no estate planning exemption. Talk with an attorney before choosing a deed type.

Who covers the stamp tax on a deed?

The contract can assign it, though the state looks to every party. The clerk collects at recording.

Is a deed valid if the clerk's recording was imperfect?

Generally yes. Section 695.26(4) says a clerk's failure to follow the recording checklist does not impair the recording or its constructive notice. Fix defects anyway, because title companies will flag them.

Can a deed in lieu replace a warranty deed?

No. A deed in lieu is how a borrower hands a property to a lender, and the state lists it as taxable. A warranty deed is the normal choice in an arm's-length sale.

A Florida quitclaim deed must meet the same writing and two-witness rule as other deeds, and documentary stamp tax applies at 70 cents per $100 of consideration. A deed between spouses or former spouses in a divorce for the marital home is excepted.

Selling a house in Florida?

What does a Florida quitclaim deed actually do?

In Florida, a quitclaim deed moves the signer's share of a property to someone else and promises nothing about it. If a lien, an unknown heir or a boundary dispute clouds the title, the new owner inherits that problem along with the house.

That lack of a promise explains where these deeds show up: a husband adding a wife to title, a parent funding a family trust, or one spouse leaving title after a divorce. A buyer paying market price from a stranger typically wants a warranty deed or a special warranty deed, and the buyer's lender or title insurer will often insist on one.

The label does not relax Florida's execution, recording or tax rules. Those apply to a quitclaim exactly as they do to any other deed.

How must a quitclaim deed be signed and witnessed in Florida?

The deed must be written and signed before two subscribing witnesses, with no seal required, and Florida lets the witnessing take place by audio-video technology (s. 689.01).

Getting it recorded takes more. Under s. 695.26, a circuit court clerk will record the instrument only if it shows:

  • each signer's printed name and a post-office address;
  • the preparer's name and address, who must be a natural person;
  • each witness's printed name and address, and the printed name of any notary beneath the notary's signature;
  • reserved room at the top right corner for the clerk: 3 by 3 inches on page one, 1 by 3 inches on later pages;
  • the grantee's name and address.

The section carves out instruments signed outside Florida, wills, plats and court orders. If a clerk records a deed that misses an item, the recording stays valid. Even so, the clerk's counter is where a noncompliant deed gets turned away, so run through the list before you go.

Is documentary stamp tax due on a quitclaim deed?

Yes. The state revenue agency's list of taxable deeds names quit claim deeds next to warranty, special warranty, trustee's and life estate deeds, and the statute sets 70 cents per $100 of consideration (s. 201.02).

Consideration reaches past a cash price. It includes anything paid, any debt released, and any mortgage or encumbrance on the parcel whether or not the grantee assumes it. A house given away with a loan still attached can therefore produce a taxable base.

As the Department of Revenue, every party to the instrument is liable no matter who agreed to pay, and an exempt party's share falls to a non-exempt one. Pay at the clerk's window when recording; if a taxable deed is never recorded, the tax is owed straight to the agency.

The same page adds that no specific exemption covers transfers made for estate planning, so deeding your own home into a revocable trust may still be taxed. Check with the clerk or a Florida attorney first.

Which quitclaim transfers are exempt, and what do the fees look like?

The state's tax page names two exempt situations: a spousal homestead deed where the only consideration is a mortgage, and a deed for the marital home delivered in a divorce (s. 201.02(7)). The same page lists a personal representative's deed under a probated will as not taxable.

Recording has its own price list. The clerk's schedule in s. 28.24 is summarized below.

Source: Florida Statutes, s. 28.24. Ask the clerk in your county for the total on a specific deed, since the page count and the number of names change it.

Does a quitclaim deed change the property tax bill?

It can. Florida treats a sale, foreclosure or any other move of legal or beneficial title as a change of ownership, so assessed value resets to just value on the next January 1 unless an exception applies (DOR Save Our Homes guidance).

Statutory exceptions include a transfer where the same person remains entitled to the benefit, a transfer between spouses, and a deed correcting an error (s. 193.155). The house with the longest ownership and the lowest assessed value stands to lose the most from an accidental reset.

Homestead exemption is a separate track: Form DR-501 is due at the property appraiser's office by March 1, and the owner must have made the house the permanent home by January 1. Talk to the appraiser before putting anyone else on a homestead deed.

When is a quitclaim deed the wrong tool for selling a Florida house?

Any sale where the buyer pays real money and expects protection calls for a different deed. A quitclaim carries no warranty, so title insurers are often reluctant to cover a purchase that rests on one.

Typical ways an owner gets stuck after using one:

  • Several heirs hold the house and one of them signs alone. A quitclaim passes only that one heir's share.
  • A mortgage is still on the property. The deed does not remove the loan, and the lender is not bound by the transfer.
  • A relative is added to the deed to avoid probate. The transfer is immediate, so the relative becomes a co-owner whose signature is needed to sell.
  • The owner wants to keep control during life. A different instrument, the enhanced life estate deed, is built for that.

On that last point, a Department of Revenue advisement (TAA 20B4-004, October 2020) concluded that a lady bird deed in the situation described did not transfer a present beneficial interest and so was not subject to documentary stamp tax. That conclusion rested on the facts presented, so confirm how it applies to yours.

How can an owner sell a Florida house when the title is messy?

First establish who legally owns the house, then repair gaps with the instrument that fits. A quitclaim deed can remove a cooperative person's name, yet it cannot manufacture ownership nobody held.

With an inherited house and several heirs, the probate court generally has to authorize the transfer. Delinquent taxes or a lien have to be paid from the sale. A buyer taking the house in current condition can absorb repairs and clutter, yet a missing signature still stops the closing.

Gather the deeds, any mortgage statement, the latest tax bill and a list of everyone who might hold an interest. A title company can then say quickly what it needs.

Frequently asked questions

Does Florida require an attorney to prepare a quitclaim deed?

Florida law does not make an attorney a condition of signing, but the deed must satisfy the two-witness rule and the recording checklist in ss. 689.01 and 695.26. Tax and title consequences follow, so many owners hire a Florida attorney or title company anyway.

Who is liable for doc stamps on a quitclaim deed?

Every party to the instrument is liable under the Department of Revenue's description, whichever party agreed to pay. The clerk collects the tax at recording.

What rate applies to a Florida deed?

The statute sets 70 cents per $100 of consideration. The Department of Revenue notes that Miami-Dade County has a different base rate plus a surtax, and the surtax is not due on a document transferring only a single-family dwelling.

Can a quitclaim deed change my homestead assessment?

Yes. A transfer of title counts as a change of ownership unless an exception in s. 193.155 applies, and the property resets to just value the following January 1.

Is a quitclaim deed the same as a lady bird deed?

No. A quitclaim deed passes the signer's interest now, while a lady bird deed keeps life-time control with the owner. The Department of Revenue advisement on lady bird deeds turned on the powers the life tenants kept.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

When a Florida owner dies without a valid will, the surviving spouse takes the entire intestate estate if the decedent left no descendants, and shares change when descendants exist. Undevised homestead follows its own rule.

Selling a house in Florida?
Get My Cash Offer →

Who gets a Florida house if the owner left no will?

The owner's spouse and descendants come first, then parents, then siblings, then more distant kin, following the order in Chapter 732 of the Florida Statutes. The path depends on who survives, and a house that qualifies as homestead follows an extra set of rules.

Intestate describes an owner who died with no valid will, or with a will that leaves the property out. The Probate Code then picks the people who take title. A sale needs someone with court-given authority to sign the deed, so the order of heirs matters mainly for knowing who gets the sale proceeds and who must agree.

How much of the estate does a surviving spouse take?

It depends on the children. Section 732.102 gives the spouse all of the intestate estate in some family setups and only half in others.

  • No surviving descendants of the decedent: the spouse takes the entire intestate estate.
  • Every descendant of the decedent is also a descendant of the spouse, and the spouse has no other descendants: the spouse takes everything.
  • The decedent had at least one descendant who is not the spouse's descendant: the spouse takes one-half.
  • All of the decedent's descendants are shared with the spouse, but the spouse has other descendants from outside the marriage: the spouse takes one-half.

Blended families are where disputes start. A second spouse with their own children from an earlier relationship cuts the surviving spouse's share to half, even when every child of the decedent is also the spouse's child.

Who inherits after the spouse's share, or when there is no spouse?

Section 732.103 sets a ladder, and each step applies only if the one above it is empty. Whatever the spouse does not take, or the whole estate when there is no spouse, passes down this list.

  1. The decedent's descendants.
  2. The father and mother equally, or the survivor of them.
  3. Brothers and sisters, with the descendants of any who died.
  4. Grandparents and then aunts, uncles and their descendants, split between the paternal and maternal sides, half to each.
  5. Kindred of the last deceased spouse, as if that spouse had survived and then died without a will.

When one side of the family has no living kin, the estate goes to the other side. The statute's last clause, written for descendants of Holocaust victims, applies only to escheated property and stopped applying to proceedings filed after December 31, 2004.

What happens to the family home when the owner leaves a spouse and children?

The spouse gets a life estate and the children get the remainder, unless the spouse elects a different split. Section 732.401 covers homestead property the owner did not leave by a valid devise.

The default is a life estate for the surviving spouse with a vested remainder to the decedent's descendants alive at death, divided per stirpes. A life tenant can live in the house but cannot hand the whole title to a buyer alone, which is why these homes often stall at sale time.

The spouse may instead elect an undivided one-half interest as a tenant in common, with the other half going to the descendants. The election must be made within 6 months after death and during the spouse's lifetime, is irrevocable once made, and is made by recording a sworn notice of election with the county clerk where the home sits. If the spouse is incapacitated, an attorney in fact or guardian needs court approval first, and the petition must also be filed within the 6 months.

Property the decedent held as tenants by the entireties, or with a co-owner under a survivorship arrangement, is outside this section.

How do heirs actually sell an inherited house?

They open a probate estate, get a personal representative appointed, and sell through that representative, or, for small estates, use a shorter court procedure.

Summary administration under section 735.201 fits an estate whose non-exempt assets stay at or below $150,000, or one where the owner has been gone over two years. Where only exempt property and a limited amount of other personal property remain, section 735.301 allows a court to authorize a transfer without full administration. Houses seldom qualify. Put the question to the probate clerk or a probate attorney.

Creditors have a limited window. Section 733.702 bars a claim that is not filed by the later of two dates: 3 months after the notice to creditors is first published, or 30 days after a creditor entitled to direct service receives it. Buyers and title companies look for that clock and for a recorded order or letters of administration before they close.

No spouse or descendants732.103(2)Parents, then siblings

Source: Florida Statutes 732.102 and 732.103, 2026 edition.

What tax and deed costs come up when heirs sell?

Heirs face three kinds of cost on a sale: deed tax, clerk recording charges and property tax changes. The state estate tax ended with federal changes for deaths after 2004, and since July 2023 personal representatives skip the DR-312 and DR-313 filings.

The deed from the estate to a buyer is a taxable document. Section 201.02 puts the deed tax at 70 cents per $100 of consideration, and every party to the document is liable, whoever agrees to pay. The agency's doc stamp page flags that no specific exemption exists for estate planning transfers, so even a quitclaim among siblings can be taxed. A deed from the personal representative under a probated will sits on its not-taxable list.

Clerk recording charges are set in section 28.24, and the clerk's office can quote the total for your deed's page count.

On property tax, a title transfer sends the assessment back to just value at the following January 1, and certain transfers upon death are carved out. Heirs who rent the home lose homestead, which the appraiser's office can confirm.

Frequently asked questions

Does a surviving spouse always inherit the whole house in Florida?

No. The spouse takes everything only when the decedent has no descendants or when all descendants are shared with the spouse. If a descendant is not the spouse's, section 732.102 gives the spouse one-half. For a homestead with a spouse and descendants, section 732.401 usually gives the spouse a life estate instead of full title.

Can a surviving spouse choose half of the homestead instead of a life estate?

Yes. The spouse may elect an undivided one-half share, held in common with the descendants, within 6 months after death and during the spouse's lifetime. The election is irrevocable and is recorded as a sworn notice in the county where the home is located.

Who inherits if there is no spouse and no children?

The parents take equally, or the survivor of them. If neither survives, the estate goes to siblings and the descendants of deceased siblings, then to grandparent and aunt and uncle lines split between the paternal and maternal sides.

Is summary administration available for a house?

It can be, when the non-exempt estate does not exceed $150,000 or the owner has been dead more than 2 years under section 735.201. Whether a given house qualifies depends on the estate's value and the court's order, so check with the probate clerk or an attorney.

Is there a Florida estate tax on inherited homes?

No. Florida has no estate tax for people dead after 2004, and personal representatives no longer file Form DR-312 or DR-313. Documentary stamp tax can still apply to deeds, and the agency treats a deed from a personal representative as not taxable when a will was probated.

What is the Florida probate process for a home?

Probate is the court-supervised step that gives someone legal authority over a dead owner's property, and a Florida house usually cannot be sold or retitled by an heir until that authority exists. The court names a personal representative, and that person handles notices, creditor claims and the eventual deed.

Which track applies depends on the size and makeup of the estate. Florida has a no-administration option for very small personal-property estates, a summary route for modest ones, and full formal administration for the rest.

Which probate track fits an inherited Florida house?

The lightest track rarely reaches a house. Under s. 735.301, no administration is available only where what remains is exempt personal property and a limited amount of other personal property, so a home generally pushes the estate into summary or formal administration.

  • No administration: personal property only, with the court approving a transfer on an informal application.
  • Summary administration: open when the non-exempt estate is $150,000 or less, or when the owner has been dead more than 2 years (s. 735.201).
  • Formal administration: the standard route for larger estates, contested wills or a house that must be sold through a personal representative.

The statute page for s. 735.201 shows a 2026 amendment, so confirm the current text with the probate clerk before relying on a threshold.

What notices must the personal representative send?

The personal representative must promptly serve a notice of administration on the surviving spouse, the beneficiaries and anyone who may be entitled to exempt property (s. 733.212). Heirs under an older will can be served too.

That notice starts several clocks. An interested person who is served has 3 months from service to object to the will's validity, the venue or the court's jurisdiction. A person who may claim exempt property must petition by the later of 4 months after service or 40 days after related litigation ends. A surviving spouse who wants an elective share generally files by the earlier of 6 months after service or 2 years after the death, unless the court extends it.

Objections to validity, venue or jurisdiction are cut off no later than the earlier of the personal representative's final discharge or 1 year after service. Buyers and title companies often wait for the objection window to pass before closing on an estate house.

The notice itself must give the decedent's name, the file number, the court and its address, whether the estate is testate or intestate and, if there is a will, its date. It also names the personal representative and that person's attorney, so heirs know whom to contact about the house.

What are the creditor claim deadlines in Florida?

A creditor must file a claim by the later of 3 months after the first publication of the notice to creditors or 30 days after being served, if that creditor had to be served (s. 733.702). Claims filed after that are barred.

A separate outer limit sits in s. 733.710: 2 years after a person's death, the estate, the personal representative and the beneficiaries are no longer liable for claims against the decedent, with an exception for a creditor who filed on time and has not been paid. A recorded mortgage or security interest is not wiped out by that limit, so the lender can still foreclose.

Does Florida charge an estate tax?

No. Revenue's estate tax page says the federal change ended Florida's estate tax for anyone who died after December 31, 2004. Since July 1, 2023, estates also skip Forms DR-312 and DR-313.

Inheriting a home can still create other costs. The county reassesses at just value after a change of ownership, which can lift a bill that was held down by the Save Our Homes cap.

Can unpaid taxes threaten an inherited house while the estate is open?

Yes, since the tax calendar keeps running during a case. A tax certificate can be sold on an unpaid account after the delinquency date, and the collector can tell the personal representative what is owed and which payment months carry a discount. Keeping the account clear protects the title for a later buyer.

How do probate steps affect selling an inherited Florida home?

The sale usually waits for the court to issue authority to the personal representative, who then signs the deed. Revenue's stamp tax page treats the estate representative's deed as a non-taxable deed, unlike an ordinary sale between living owners.

Probate time limits that touch a house sale

Outer claim bar2 years after deaths. 733.710

After authority is in place, the family can list the house or sell it directly.

Which county offices matter when an estate holds a Florida house?

Florida has 67 counties, and each elects its own clerk, property appraiser and tax collector. An estate with a house deals with all three, so the county of the property matters more than where the heirs live.

  • County clerk: handles the probate file, records the deed and collects documentary stamp tax at recording.
  • Property appraiser: sets just value each January 1 and decides whether a homestead exemption or other benefit applies.
  • Tax collector: sends the November bill, takes payment and sells tax certificates on unpaid accounts.

The deed that ends the estate must meet the same form rules as any Florida conveyance. Florida also requires land conveyances to carry two witnesses (s. 689.01). A title company reviewing an estate sale checks that detail alongside the court order.

What should heirs do before the house is sold?

Start by locating the original will and asking the county clerk where the home stands where it should be filed. Then plan around the property itself while the case runs.

  • Keep the property taxes and insurance current, since the bill keeps arriving whether or not title has moved.
  • Ask the property appraiser whether a homestead exemption was in place, because it ends when the owner no longer lives there as a permanent resident.
  • Ask the tax collector about the discount months and the delinquency date.
  • Wait on any contract until the personal representative has written authority.

Is probate unavoidable for an inherited house?

Often it is, when the dead owner held the house alone and no other transfer device applies. Real property falls outside the no-administration track meant for small personal-property estates. Ask the probate clerk or a Florida lawyer which track fits.

How much can an estate be worth to use summary administration?

The non-exempt estate may not exceed $150,000, or the decedent must have been dead more than 2 years (s. 735.201). The statute page shows a 2026 amendment, so check the current wording with the clerk.

What cutoff do creditors face?

They must file by the later of 3 months after first publication of the notice to creditors or 30 days after service, where service was required (s. 733.702). Two years after death, s. 733.710 cuts off most remaining claims against the estate.

Will the estate owe Florida estate tax?

No. Florida's estate tax ended for deaths after December 31, 2004, and DR-312 and DR-313 have been unnecessary since July 1, 2023.

Does a deed from the estate carry stamp tax?

Revenue lists a deed from a personal representative under a probated will as not taxable. It adds that estate-planning transfers in general have no specific exemption, so check other deeds with the clerk.

Florida Homestead Protection: Devise Limits, Spouse Waivers and Selling

Cash Home Buyers in Florida
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
