  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Florida Homestead Protection sale
  • Turn the Florida Homestead Protection offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Florida Homestead? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is and coordinate with the title company on spouse signatures.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Florida homestead is exempt from forced sale under court process, and it cannot be devised if the owner is survived by a spouse or minor child, with limited exceptions. A spouse who must join the deed has specific waiver language under Sec. 732.702.

Selling a house in Florida?
Get My Cash Offer →

How does Florida protect a homestead from creditors?

Article X, section 4 of the Florida Constitution shields a natural person's homestead from forced sale under court process, so no judgment, decree or execution becomes a lien on it. The shield has three carve-outs: taxes and assessments, debts incurred to buy, improve or repair the property, and debts for labor performed on the realty (Florida Constitution, Art. X, s. 4).

The size limit depends on location. Outside a municipality the protected homestead may reach 160 contiguous acres. Inside one, it is one-half acre of contiguous land, and the protection is limited to the residence of the owner or the owner's family. Personal property up to $1,000 gets the same shield, and the protection passes to a surviving spouse or heirs.

Can a Florida homestead be left to anyone in a will?

Not when the owner leaves a spouse or a minor child. The Constitution bars a devise in that case, with one exception: the homestead may go to the spouse if there is no minor child. Section 732.4015 repeats the rule (Florida Statutes, s. 732.4015).

Trusts do not sidestep it. The statute defines "devise" to include a trust disposition of the part of the trust estate that would be homestead if titled in the grantor's name, and it treats the grantor of a qualifying trust as the owner. If a spouse's devised interest is disclaimed, it passes under chapter 739.

For heirs preparing to sell, the practical point is that a will may not control who holds title. The closing agent will ask who survived the owner before it insures a sale.

Who owns the house when the owner dies without a valid devise?

It descends as ordinary intestate property, with a twist for spouses. If the owner left a spouse and descendants, the spouse takes a life estate and the descendants take a vested remainder. Section 732.401 lets the spouse swap that for an undivided one-half interest as a tenant in common, with the other half vesting in the descendants.

The swap has strict mechanics, all from the statute (Florida Statutes, s. 732.401):

  • The election must be made within 6 months after death and during the spouse's lifetime.
  • An attorney in fact or guardian needs court approval, and the petition must also be filed within the 6 months.
  • Once made, the election is irrevocable.
  • It is made by recording a notice of election, with the legal description, in the county's official records.

Until the election is made or the window closes, a buyer cannot be sure what interest the spouse holds. Sellers in this position should bring the recorded notice, or proof none was filed, to the title company early.

Does a married owner need a spouse's signature to sell?

Yes. The Constitution says the owner of homestead real estate, joined by the spouse if married, may alienate the homestead by mortgage, sale or gift. A deed signed by one spouse alone leaves a gap that a title insurer will flag.

The same sentence lets a married owner deed the property into a tenancy by the entirety with the spouse. If the owner or spouse is incompetent, the method of alienation follows what the law provides, which usually means a court or guardian is involved.

Conveyances of land also need to be in writing and signed before two subscribing witnesses under s. 689.01. Have the closing agent review the witness blocks.

What does a spouse's waiver actually waive?

Less than many people assume. Section 732.7025 supplies deed language by which a spouse gives up the devise restriction, allowing the owner to leave the home to someone other than that spouse. Language "substantially similar" to the statute's wording is enough.

The statute then draws two lines (Florida Statutes, s. 732.7025). That waiver does not give up protection against the owner's creditors during life or after death. It also does not remove the restriction on selling, mortgaging or gifting the homestead without the spouse's joinder.

A broader waiver exists in s. 732.702. A surviving spouse's rights to homestead, elective share, intestate share, family allowance and more may be waived by a written agreement signed in front of two subscribing witnesses. Waivers made after marriage require fair disclosure of the signer's estate. A waiver of "all rights" in a property settlement reaches homestead unless it says otherwise (Florida Statutes, s. 732.702).

How do the two waiver statutes compare?

They do different jobs, and sellers often mix them up. This table sets them side by side.

Features. 732.7025 deed waivers. 732.702 written waiver
Where it appearsIn a deedStand-alone contract, agreement or waiver
ScopeDevise restriction onlyHomestead and other spousal rights, wholly or partly
WitnessesStatute prescribes the deed languageTwo subscribing witnesses
Effect on joinder to sellNone, joinder still requiredDepends on the waiver's terms

Source: the two statute pages linked above. A lawyer should draft or review either one.

How does a Florida homestead affect a sale after probate or divorce?

Both events can change who must sign. After a death, check whether the homestead passed by intestacy, whether a spouse made the six-month election, and whether the estate needs administration. Summary administration is available when the non-exempt estate does not exceed $150,000 or the decedent has been dead more than two years (s. 735.201). Creditor claims are barred after the later of three months from first publication of the notice to creditors or 30 days after service on a creditor who must be served (s. 733.702).

Divorce is a separate path. The Constitution's joinder rule still applies to any sale made before the court rules on the marital home, so a buyer's title agent will want the final judgment or the spouse's signature.

Documentary stamp tax rules also apply. The Department of Revenue lists a personal representative's deed under a probated will is not taxable, and divorce deeds for the marital home and spousal homestead deeds where the only consideration is a mortgage are exempt under s. 201.02(7) (Department of Revenue, documentary stamp tax).

What should an heir or seller gather for a homestead closing?

Title work on a homestead depends on documents showing who held title and who survived. Collect them before the contract goes out.

  • The death certificate and the deed that put the owner on title.
  • Any will or trust instrument, since a trust counts as a devise for homestead purposes.
  • A recorded notice of election if a spouse chose the one-half interest.
  • Any marital agreement or waiver signed before two subscribing witnesses.
  • Divorce judgments that award the marital home.

The constitutional protection also runs to heirs. It inures to the surviving spouse or heirs of the owner, so creditors of the deceased owner face the same limits that applied during life, apart from the listed exceptions for taxes, purchase and improvement debts, and labor on the property.

A short call to the clerk of the circuit court clarifies how recorded documents will appear in the official records, and the clerk's recording charges are set by s. 28.24.

Frequently asked questions

Is a Florida homestead safe from judgment creditors?

Generally yes. A court judgment cannot become a lien on it, but taxes, purchase or improvement debts and labor on the property are exceptions. The shield covers up to 160 acres outside a municipality or one-half acre inside one.

Can I leave my Florida homestead to my children if I am married?

Not by will or trust devise. If a spouse survives you, the homestead cannot be devised to someone else unless the spouse waived that restriction. A devise to the spouse is allowed only if no minor child survives.

Does my wife or husband have to sign the deed to sell?

Yes, on a homestead. The Constitution has the owner joined by the spouse when selling, mortgaging or gifting. Skipping the spouse leaves the deed open to challenge.

How long does a surviving spouse have to elect a half interest?

Six months from the date of death, and the election must be made during the spouse's lifetime. It is irrevocable and made by recording a notice of election with the clerk of that county.

Does the deed waiver language let me sell without my spouse?

No. Section 732.7025 waives only the devise restriction. It does not waive creditor protection or the requirement that a spouse join in any sale, mortgage or gift.

Facing Florida Foreclosure? Get a Cash Offer Before the Sale

How does a foreclosure work in Florida?

Florida foreclosures go through a court. The lender files suit, a judge enters a final judgment, and the circuit court clerk sells the home at a public sale. The owner can stop that sale at several points, and one of them is a sale of the house on the owner's own terms.

The process rests on Chapter 45 and Chapter 702 of the Florida Statutes. Chapter 45 covers the sale itself and the right to cure, and section 702.10 covers a faster path some lenders use through an order to show cause.

A homeowner served with a complaint should study every date on it and speak with a Florida attorney soon. Delay seldom helps.

What happens after the judge enters a final judgment?

The judgment tells the clerk to sell the property at public sale. Under section 45.031, the sale takes place not less than 20 days or more than 35 days after the judgment, unless the plaintiff agrees to a later date.

Notice goes out on a website under section 50.0311 for at least two consecutive weeks, or in a newspaper once a week for two consecutive weeks. The clerk may run the sale electronically.

  • The top bidder puts up 5 percent of the bid as a deposit.
  • The clerk files a certificate of sale.
  • If nobody objects within 10 days, the clerk files the certificate of title and the sale stands confirmed.

The law treats the winning bid as sufficient consideration, so a later argument about price faces a hard road.

Can I stop a Florida foreclosure sale?

Yes, up to a point. Section 45.0315 lets the mortgagor, or the holder of a subordinate interest, cure the debt and stop the sale at any time before the later of the clerk's filing of the certificate of sale or the time stated in the judgment.

The cure is paying the amount stated in the judgment. If no judgment exists yet, the owner tenders the performance due under the security agreement, including accelerated amounts, plus the lender's reasonable expenses of foreclosing, which include reasonable attorney's fees.

The statute then closes the door: after that moment, there is no right of redemption. A homeowner who is counting on a post sale redemption period will not find one in this section.

What is the order to show cause route?

Section 702.10 lets a lienholder ask for an order to show cause by filing a verified complaint. The hearing may be held no sooner than the later of 20 days after service of the order or 45 days after service of the complaint.

The resulting judgment operates against the property only, and a deficiency may still be allowed where the law permits it. The statute also says attorney fees up to 3 percent of principal need no reasonableness hearing.

One limit helps owners who live in the home. The payment or vacate order does not apply to owner occupied residences, and a granted homestead exemption on the latest tax roll is a rebuttable presumption that the home is owner occupied. See section 702.10 for the full text.

What numbers and dates matter most?

What happens to money left over after the sale?

If the sale brings in more than the debt and costs, the extra is surplus funds. The final judgment has to carry a notice about them, and a homeowner is told to check with the clerk within 10 days after the sale.

Claims for surplus must be filed before the clerk reports the funds as unclaimed. Other lienholders may also claim a share, so the clerk's file is the place to look before assuming anything is owed.

What should I do when I get a foreclosure complaint?

Read the summons for the response deadline and act inside it. A missed response can let the lender move toward judgment without your side being heard.

  • Collect the mortgage, note, payment history and any letters from the servicer.
  • Ask the circuit court clerk how to find your case on the docket.
  • Ask for the payoff in writing, since the cure under section 45.0315 depends on the amount in the judgment or the tender due.
  • Speak with a Florida attorney or a housing counselor before agreeing to anything.

Keeping a line open to the lender's attorney preserves choices, including a sale before the clerk fixes a date.

How do taxes and recording costs enter a foreclosure?

The certificate of title that follows a sale is on the state's list of taxable documents. Section 201.02(9) figures that tax on the highest and best bid at the sale.

Property taxes are separate. A change of ownership, including a foreclosure, resets the property to just value on the following January 1 for assessment, per the Department of Revenue's Save Our Homes guide. Owners who lose the home also lose the homestead exemption benefit, which is tied to permanent residence.

What does a sale before the auction look like?

A sale in the open market or to a cash buyer settles the lender's payoff out of the money at the table, and the foreclosure case can then be dismissed. A deed in that sale carries the stamp tax of 70 cents per $100 in most counties, and the state treats every party to the deed as liable whichever side agrees to pay.

The timing target is the sale date the clerk has set. If a buyer can close ahead of it, the owner avoids a sale at auction and keeps control of the price. If it cannot, ask the lender's attorney whether the sale can be postponed. The plaintiff may consent to a date longer than 35 days.

Have the title agent confirm the payoff, junior liens and unpaid property tax before you sign a contract.

What are my options before the sale date?

An owner facing foreclosure has several paths, and each one has a different effect on timing and cost.

  • Cure the debt under section 45.0315 before the cutoff.
  • Sell the house before the sale, which pays the lender from the proceeds and avoids a sale at auction.
  • Hand the lender a deed in lieu, a transfer the state revenue agency counts as a taxable deed.
  • Contest the case in court with an attorney's help.

Cash buyers often move quicker than a retail listing, which matters while the post judgment window is running. Call the clerk's office for the sale date, and get the lender's attorney to put the payoff in writing first.

Frequently asked questions

How long after judgment is a Florida foreclosure sale held?

The sale is set for not less than 20 days and not more than 35 days after the final judgment, unless the plaintiff agrees to a longer period.

Is there a redemption period after the sale in Florida?

No. Section 45.0315 gives a right to cure only until the later of the certificate of sale or the time in the judgment, and then states that there is no right of redemption.

Who runs the foreclosure sale?

The circuit court clerk. The clerk may conduct it electronically, publishes the notice, files the certificate of sale and later the certificate of title.

What is the deposit on a foreclosure bid?

The high bidder posts a deposit of 5 percent of the final bid, and objections are due within 10 days of the certificate.

Can I get surplus money after the sale?

Possibly. Surplus claims must be filed before the clerk reports the funds as unclaimed, and a homestead owner should check with the clerk within 10 days after the sale.

Want a Sale With No Closing Costs to You? Get a Cash Offer

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling a house in Florida?

Which closing costs hit a Florida seller?

On the statute side, the big items are the stamp tax on the deed, the clerk's recording charges, title work and the seller's slice of the year's property tax. Commissions, repair credits and association fees come from the contract, not from state law. Florida contracts leave much of this open, so the signed paper decides who pays each line.

This page covers the charges that a Florida statute or the Department of Revenue puts in writing. Ask your title agent or closing attorney to explain any other charge on the settlement sheet before you sign.

What does the deed stamp tax come to?

The statutory rate is seventy cents for every $100 of consideration, counting any part of a hundred, in every county but Miami-Dade. Section 201.02 states it, and the revenue agency's page repeats it. Consideration is a wide term: cash, a debt you are released from, and any mortgage or encumbrance on the parcel all count, whether or not the buyer assumes the loan.

Miami-Dade prints sixty cents per $100 plus a 45 cent surtax per $100. The surtax is skipped when the paper transfers only a single-family dwelling, so the clerk in that county can tell you which version fits your deed.

The clerk collects it at recording. A deed is taxable recorded or not, and a taxable paper that never gets recorded is paid to the Department itself. After a foreclosure sale, the certificate of title is taxed on the highest and best bid, per section 201.02(9).

Who is responsible for paying doc stamps?

Your contract names the payer, yet the state treats everyone on the document as liable. The agency's page says liability stays with all parties whichever one agreed to pay, and a non-exempt party covers the tax when another party is exempt. No statute assigns the deed tax to a particular side.

If you agreed to pay, expect the title agent to subtract the tax from your proceeds at the table. The Department lists these exemptions and exclusions:

  • A spousal homestead deed where a mortgage is the only consideration.
  • A divorce deed for the marital home.
  • A deed by a personal representative acting under a probated will, which the Department lists as not taxable.

How does the buyer's loan change the picture?

Mortgages and notes are taxed separately from the deed. The Department prints 35 cents on each $100 secured, with the note tax limited to $2,450 and no limit on mortgages. These charges follow the buyer's financing, so an all-cash buyer has none of them.

On your side, a lender holding your own mortgage will want payoff in full at closing. Order a written payoff statement a few days ahead, since interest accrues daily and the figure moves.

What are the clerk's recording fees?

Under section 28.24, an instrument of ordinary size costs $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 for every added page, with a $1.00 charge for each name past the fourth. A trust fund charge of $1.00 on page one and 50 cents on later pages sits on top, plus a $4 per page technology charge.

That adds up to far less than the stamp tax. A long deed with many grantors costs more than a short one, so have the closing agent quote the recording total before closing.

Does the seller pay for title insurance?

Whoever pays, the premium schedule comes from state rule. Florida's rule on title insurance rates cites sections 627.782 and 627.7825 as its authority. Your contract names the party who buys the owner's policy, so read its title paragraph.

Section 627.7841 gives one protection worth knowing. If the insurer's own officers, employees or agents disburse your closing funds, the insurer must cover defects recorded after the commitment date and ahead of recording the deed, except those the insured knows about. That is a reason to close through a title agent who handles the money.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How must the deed be signed in Florida?

A deed that conveys a freehold or a lease of more than one year has to be written and signed before two subscribing witnesses, under section 689.01. No seal is needed. The statute allows the witnessing to happen by audio-video technology, which helps an owner who has moved out of state before closing.

Ask the title agent to send the deed for review before the closing date, so a missing witness or a misspelled name does not push the closing back.

What do condo and HOA sellers pay at closing?

A seller in an association community also orders an estoppel certificate. For a condominium, section 718.116 lets the association charge a reasonable fee of no more than $250 when nothing is delinquent, plus $100 for delivery within 3 business days and up to $150 more when money is owed. The homeowners' association statute, 720.30851, uses the same figures. The caps are adjusted every five years, so check the Department of Business and Professional Regulation website for the current amounts.

A separate guide on selling a condo or HOA home covers the estoppel timeline and the documents a condo seller must hand over.

What should a Florida seller collect before closing?

Gather the items that drive the final numbers and ask for each in writing.

  • A payoff letter from every lender or lienholder, dated close to closing.
  • An estoppel certificate if the home is in a condominium or homeowners' association.
  • The current tax bill from the tax collector, so the proration is checked against a real figure.
  • The proposed settlement statement a few days early, with the deed tax line matched to your contract price.
  • The recorded deed once the clerk returns it.

A buyer planning to claim homestead must file with the appraiser's office by March 1, and the state says a change of ownership resets the assessment to just value the following January 1. That reassessment is the buyer's concern, but it explains why buyers ask sellers for tax details.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What happens with property taxes and listing disclosures?

Tax bills arrive in November and carry an early-payment discount that steps down month by month until February. Unpaid taxes turn delinquent on April 1. The closing agent normally divides the annual bill with the buyer as the contract directs, and the tax collector can give you the current amount.

Residential buyers must get a property tax disclosure at or before signing under section 689.261. It warns that the seller's present bill is a poor guide, because a sale or new improvements triggers reassessment. The statute adds that from February 1, 2027, listing materials may not show the current owner's tax amount, so ask your agent how your listing will read.

Who ends up paying the deed stamps?

Whoever your contract says, though the state holds every party liable. Liability stays with all parties on the document, per the revenue agency. Read the closing cost paragraph for the agreed payer.

Will a cash buyer owe the mortgage tax?

No. That tax applies to mortgages and notes at 35 cents per $100 secured, and a cash purchase creates neither. Only the deed tax and recording charges remain.

Is Miami-Dade different?

Yes. The Department prints 60 cents per $100 plus a 45 cent surtax, and the surtax is not due on a paper transferring only a single-family dwelling.

How much is recording a deed?

Under section 28.24 page one costs $5.00 and added pages cost $4.00 each, with a trust fund charge, a $4 per page technology charge and $1.00 per name past four.

When do property tax bills come and go delinquent?

Bills are mailed in November, and unpaid ones become delinquent on April 1. Your closing agent prorates the year with the buyer.

Which disclosures must a Florida home seller give?

A Florida seller of residential property owes the buyer three statutory notices: a flood disclosure, a property tax summary and a radon notice. A licensed agent has an added duty to reveal known hidden defects that affect value.

Each notice has its own deadline, and each is tied to the moment the contract is signed. Giving them late, or leaving one out, is the kind of slip that invites a dispute at closing. This guide walks through them in the order they usually arise.

What does the Florida flood disclosure say?

Section 689.302 requires the seller to complete and give the buyer a flood disclosure at or before the time the sales contract is executed (s. 689.302). The statute prints the form, which opens with a warning that homeowners' insurance policies do not include coverage for flood damage and encourages the buyer to talk to an insurance agent about separate flood coverage.

The seller then answers three checkbox questions:

  • whether the seller has knowledge of any flooding that damaged the property during the seller's ownership;
  • whether the seller has filed an insurance claim for flood damage, including a claim under the National Flood Insurance Program;
  • whether the seller has received assistance for flood damage, including assistance from FEMA.

The form defines flooding as a general or temporary condition of partial or complete inundation. It lists three causes: overflow of inland or tidal waters, unusual and rapid buildup of runoff or surface water from a source such as a river, stream or drainage ditch, and sustained standing water after rainfall. The statute's history shows amendments in 2024 and 2025.

Answer from your own records. If you cannot recall whether a claim was filed, check old insurance correspondence before you tick a box.

What is the property tax disclosure summary?

The buyer must receive a property tax disclosure summary at or before signing, either built into the contract or attached to it (s. 689.261). Unless the contract includes it, the seller must provide it.

Its message is that the buyer should not rely on the seller's current property taxes as the amount the buyer will owe the following year, because a change of ownership or improvements trigger reassessment. The summary points questions about valuation to the county property appraiser.

If the summary is a separate document, the contract must refer to it and carry prominent language telling the buyer not to sign until the summary has been read. That reference is easy to overlook in a homemade contract.

What changes for property tax listings in 2027?

Beginning February 1, 2027, any home visible on a public listing platform must show an estimated ad valorem tax figure instead of the current owner's bill. The same date bars the current owner's taxes from printed listing materials.

The statute allows the platform to estimate by applying current millage rates to the listing price, using a formula the Department of Revenue publishes, or by using the countywide average millage rate. Either way the platform must carry a disclaimer that millage varies within a county and that the estimate leaves out non-ad valorem assessments, exemptions and the transfer of a homestead assessment difference. The Department of Revenue is to publish the formula and rate data from December 15, 2026, and annually after that. The law also says no cause of action arises against anyone for an inaccurate estimate.

For a seller, the practical effect is that listing photos and copy should not quote your own tax bill. Ask your agent how the platform will present the estimate.

What is the radon notice?

Florida requires a radon notice on at least one document signed at or before a contract for sale of any building (s. 404.056(5)). Standard contract forms normally carry it already.

The required text describes radon as a naturally occurring radioactive gas that may present health risks over time when it builds up in a building. It adds that levels above federal and state guidelines have been found in Florida buildings and that the county health department can supply information on radon and testing. Transient occupancy of 45 days or less is excluded.

Anyone who measures or mitigates radon for a fee must be certified by the state, so ask for a certification number if a buyer orders a test.

What must a seller reveal beyond the forms, and what need not be reported?

A real estate licensee working with a seller must disclose all known facts that materially affect the value of residential property and are not readily observable to the buyer (s. 475.278). The statute lists this duty for single agents, transaction brokers and licensees with no brokerage relationship alike.

Florida also draws a line on stigma. Under s. 689.25, the fact that a property was, or was suspected to have been, the site of a homicide, suicide or death is not a material fact that must be disclosed. The same holds for an occupant's HIV infection or AIDS diagnosis, and no cause of action arises against an owner or licensee for staying silent on either.

Radon noticeOn at least one document at or before contract

Source: Fla. Stat. ss. 689.302, 689.261, 404.056, 689.25. A known defect that affects value and that a buyer could not readily see falls under the licensee duty above, so tell your agent about it and put it in writing.

How do property taxes reset after the sale?

The buyer's tax bill can differ sharply from yours, which is the reason for the tax summary above. The Department of Revenue explains that a sale, foreclosure or other change of legal or beneficial title resets the property to just value the following January 1, with exceptions such as transfers between spouses (DOR Save Our Homes guidance).

The annual calendar, as the department prints it, runs like this:

  • January 1 is the assessment date.
  • March 1 is the filing deadline for exemptions and classifications with the property appraiser.
  • In August the appraiser mails the Notice of Proposed Property Taxes, and a value challenge petition is due 25 days after that notice.
  • In November the tax collector sends bills, and the department prints early-payment discounts of 4 percent in November, 3 percent in December, 2 percent in January and 1 percent in February.
  • Unpaid taxes become delinquent on April 1.

Source: Florida Department of Revenue taxpayer page. Ask the county tax collector for the status of the current bill before you list, since unpaid taxes come out of your proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

When must I give the buyer the flood disclosure?

At or before the time the sales contract is signed. Section 689.302 sets that deadline and prints the form.

Do I have to tell a buyer someone died in the house?

No. Section 689.25 says a death, homicide or suicide on the property is not a material fact that must be disclosed, and no lawsuit arises from staying silent.

Can I advertise my current property tax bill on a listing?

Not after February 1, 2027. From that date the current owner's ad valorem taxes cannot appear in printed listing materials, and listing platforms must show an estimate instead.

Is a radon notice required if my home tested low?

Yes. The notice goes on at least one document signed at or before the contract and does not depend on a test result.

Does an as-is sale remove disclosure duties?

No. The statutory notices apply to a residential sale whatever the condition, and a licensee still must disclose known material facts that the buyer cannot readily observe.

Can I sell my house without an agent in Florida?

Yes. Florida law places no licensing requirement on an owner who sells their own home, but several written disclosures and recording rules still apply to the seller.

The paperwork falls into three groups: what the buyer must be handed before the contract is signed, what the deed must look like, and what the tax and county offices need afterward. The sections below take those in order.

What disclosures must a Florida for sale by owner seller give?

Two statutory forms apply to residential sales: a property tax disclosure summary and a flood disclosure. The buyer needs each one no later than contract signing.

Written items a Florida seller hands the buyer
ItemStatuteWhat it covers
Property tax disclosure summarys. 689.261Warns the buyer not to assume the seller's tax bill carries over, since a change of ownership or improvements can trigger reassessment
Flood disclosures. 689.302Seller's knowledge of past flooding, any flood insurance claim, and any flood assistance received

If the tax summary is not built into the contract, it must be attached, and the contract must refer to it and tell the buyer not to sign until it is read.

What does the flood disclosure ask?

It opens with a notice that homeowners' policies do not cover flood damage and that the buyer should discuss separate flood coverage with an insurance agent.

  • Any flood damage you know of while you owned the home.
  • Whether the seller filed a flood damage claim, including with the National Flood Insurance Program.
  • Whether the seller received help for flood damage, including from FEMA.

The statute defines flooding as inundation from overflowing inland or tidal water, rapid runoff from an established water source such as a ditch, or sustained standing water after rainfall.

How do listing rules about property taxes change in 2027?

From February 1, 2027, online listings must display a tax estimate and printed marketing must drop the owner's present tax figure.

Section 689.261(3) says the estimate must be built from the listing price at current millage rates, or from the countywide average rate, using data the Department of Revenue publishes. The statute adds that no one is liable for an inaccurate estimate. For a seller advertising a house, this means flyers should leave out your own tax amount, and online listings will lean on the estimator instead.

What goes into the deed and closing paperwork?

The deed is a written instrument signed before two subscribing witnesses, as s. 689.01 describes, and recording under s. 695.26 needs printed names, addresses and blank margin space for the clerk.

  • A warranty deed or another deed type that matches what you promise the buyer.
  • Printed names and post-office addresses for signers, witnesses and the preparer.
  • Stamp tax paid when the deed is recorded, at the statewide deed rate (Miami-Dade has its own schedule).
  • Clerk recording charges that depend on page count.

Because every party stays liable, the contract should say who pays. A title company or attorney can run the closing if you prefer not to handle a deed alone.

How does a sale affect the tax bill and my exemption?

Bills go to whoever owns the property of record, so the settlement statement is where a year's tax gets divided.

Paying early in November earns the biggest state-printed discount, and the discount steps down each month to 1 percent in February. Because assessment returns to just value after a sale, the buyer's bill may look nothing like yours. The buyer files a fresh homestead application. Let the property appraiser know you sold, so your own exemption is cancelled.

What are the tax lien risks if I skip the closing agent?

A sale does not erase an unpaid tax bill, so a private seller should confirm the year's taxes are paid or credited at closing.

Delinquency begins April 1, and certificates on unpaid parcels are auctioned by June 1. A certificate holder waits two years before pressing the owner, and a tax deed application may follow. For a homestead, a tax deed sale opens at the amounts due plus half the latest assessed value (ss. 197.432 and 197.502). Keep the account current through closing.

In what order should a private sale proceed?

  • Prepare the property tax summary and the flood disclosure so they can be handed over with the contract.
  • Put in the contract who bears the deed tax and recording fees.
  • Prepare the deed, then sign it before two witnesses and a notary.
  • File the signed deed at the county clerk with the stamp tax.
  • Notify the property appraiser of the sale and cancel your exemptions.

When are the main property tax dates a seller should know?

  • January 1: the appraiser sets just value.
  • March 1: last timely day to apply for exemptions.
  • August: the TRIM notice arrives, and a value petition is due within 25 days.
  • November: tax bills are sent.
  • April 1: unpaid taxes turn delinquent.

Whatever the closing date, set the proration in the contract and ask the county tax collector for a payoff figure.

Should a seller order a title search?

Yes, early. A buyer's lender will want clear title, and a search shows liens, prior deeds and the exact names that must appear on the new deed. It also reveals whether the owner of record matches the people who will sign, which saves a rejected recording at the clerk's counter.

The search is also the moment to check for an old homestead exemption you forgot to cancel or a tax account carrying a deferral, since both affect the closing figures.

Can a seller still use a payment plan or deferral?

Possibly, though the sale changes things. A homestead tax deferral is requested on Form DR-570 by March 31 after the assessment year, and it covers taxes above 5 percent of household income. Installment prepayment must be requested by May 1 of the assessment year under s. 197.222, and partial payments are at the collector's discretion before the delinquency date.

Deferred or installment balances should be cleared out of the closing proceeds, so ask the tax collector for a written payoff before the closing date.

Are there other risks that FSBO sellers overlook?

Three come up often: lender liens, county tax liens and occupants.

  • Delinquent taxes lead down a path to a certificate sale, so settle the bill.
  • Occupants need proper notice before closing; section 83.57 sets 30 days for a month-to-month tenancy.
  • A buyer's lender will want clear title, so order a title search early.

Where do I record the deed after a private sale?

Record it with the clerk of the circuit court in the county where the land sits, since the clerk records documents and collects stamp tax. Bring a deed that follows the printed-name and margin rules.

Is a lawyer required for a private sale?

No statute requires one, but a Florida attorney or title company can prepare the deed, check title and handle recording. Many sellers hire one for the closing even when they find their own buyer.

Must a FSBO seller give a property tax disclosure?

Yes. Section 689.261 requires the buyer to receive the summary at or before signing the contract. It can be part of the contract or a separate attachment.

Is the flood disclosure required even if my house never flooded?

Yes, the form still goes to the buyer, and you mark that you have no knowledge of flooding, no claim and no assistance. It is due at or before contract signing under s. 689.302.

May I put my present tax bill in a flyer?

After February 1, 2027, no. Printed marketing must leave out the owner's current ad valorem taxes, and online platforms must use estimators. The appraiser's website has an estimator.

What is the yearly rhythm of a Florida property tax bill?

Everything hangs on January 1, when each county's property appraiser fixes just value for every parcel. Exemption filings follow by March 1, the TRIM notice lands in August, and the tax collector sends the actual bill in November.

Florida tax year in order, from the Department of Revenue's taxpayer page
WhenWhat happens
January 1Parcels valued at just value
March 1Last day to file for exemptions or special classifications
April 1Business owners file the DR-405 for tangible personal property
AugustTRIM notice (DR-474) goes out
Sept. to Nov.Tentative and final budget and millage hearings
NovemberBills (DR-528) mailed

A challenge to value is filed within 25 days of the TRIM notice, and a denied exemption gets 30 days from the denial letter.

How much can Florida homeowners save by paying early?

The discount shrinks one point per month, as Revenue prints it: 4 percent for November, then 3, 2 and 1 for the next three months through February. A bill paid after that window carries no discount.

Paying nothing by April 1 makes the account delinquent, and the collector sells certificates on the leftover balance by June 1 (s. 197.343).

What does a Florida homestead exemption take off the assessment?

Up to $50,000, split in two layers under s. 196.031. The first $25,000 reduces value for every levy, school levies included. The second layer of up to $25,000 reaches only assessed value above $50,000 and skips school levies. Its dollar amount grows each January 1 with CPI when CPI is positive and holds flat when negative.

  • You need to be living there as a permanent resident on January 1.
  • File Form DR-501 with the appraiser's office by March 1.
  • Renting out the home, moving out or leaving Florida ends the exemption.
  • Servicemembers may rent a homestead without losing it (s. 196.061).

How does the Save Our Homes cap behave?

A homestead gets its first year at just value. After that, its assessed value may climb each year by only the smaller of 3 percent or inflation as measured by CPI (s. 193.155), and it can never exceed just value. Revenue keeps a cap chart, revised January 2026, so check it for the latest year.

Parcels without homestead have a looser brake of 10 percent per year. Both brakes end when ownership changes, a term that includes sales, foreclosures and any other shift of legal or beneficial title.

Can the cap follow me when I buy another Florida home?

It can. Portability lets you carry the difference between just and assessed value to a new homestead, if that homestead is established within three years counted from January 1 of the year you gave up the old one. The statute reduces the new assessment by the lesser of $500,000 or that difference.

File DR-501T alongside DR-501 by March 1. The statute page flags chapter 2026-239 amendments that first apply to the 2027 roll, so call the appraiser about current limits.

How do I read my TRIM notice and November bill?

The August TRIM notice is a proposal, not a bill. It shows last year's and this year's values and the millage each taxing body proposes, along with the dates of its hearings. The November bill shows what was actually levied after those hearings.

  • Compare just value, assessed value and taxable value, since a homestead's assessed value can sit below just value.
  • Check that your exemption appears. If it is missing, ask the appraiser before the 30-day window after a denial notice runs out.
  • Check each taxing body's line, such as county, school board and city, for a change from the prior year.
  • Note the 25-day petition limit if you think value is wrong.

Call the tax collector for your parcel's payoff figure before any sale or refinance, since discounts change month by month.

Which older-owner and veteran benefits can lower a Florida bill?

These benefits mostly depend on local ordinance, so county and city of residence decide what you get.

  • Age 65 and up: a local government may add up to $50,000 for owners within an income limit (s. 196.075(2)).
  • Older veterans with permanent service-connected disability: a discount tracking the VA rating (s. 196.082).
  • Honorably discharged ex-servicemembers with a rating of 10 percent or more: $5,000 off assessed value.
  • Deployed servicemembers: a proportional exemption through Form DR-501M.

Homestead deferral is separate. Ask the tax collector about Form DR-570 before the March 31 filing date, and ask which income thresholds the office applies to your household.

Who decides the rate, and what limits it?

Each taxing body on your bill adopts millage at hearings in the fall. Tentative budget hearings come in September and October, and final ones in October and November. State law ties growth in a taxing body's property tax revenue to growth in Florida per capita personal income plus new construction, unless a super-majority, unanimous vote or referendum goes beyond that.

The August TRIM notice shows proposed millage, so it is the best moment to attend a hearing.

Can I pay in parts or push payment back?

Installment prepayment needs an application to the tax collector by May 1 of the assessment year (s. 197.222). Part payments before delinquency are the collector's call (s. 197.374).

Ask your collector which version your county runs. Installments and homestead deferral are different programs with different filing dates.

What can a delinquent Florida account lead to?

After April 1 the collector offers a certificate to the bidder who takes the lowest interest rate, bid in quarter-point steps (s. 197.432). The holder must wait 2 years from April 1 of the issuance year before asking the owner for payment, and a tax deed application can follow (s. 197.502).

The clerk then runs the public auction under s. 197.542. Homestead parcels carry a higher opening bid than other property, since half the latest assessed value is added to the amounts due. Pay before a certificate exists if you can, because every step after that adds cost.

What should a Florida buyer or heir ask about taxes?

Do not assume the seller's bill predicts yours. A long-held homestead may sit well under just value because of the cap, and that gap disappears at transfer.

  • What is the parcel's just value compared with its assessed value?
  • Is the current exemption tied to the seller's residence, and will it end at closing?
  • Are any tax certificates outstanding on the parcel?
  • Which taxing bodies levy on this address, and did any propose higher millage?

The appraiser and tax collector answer these by phone or at the counter, and the answers help you set a budget before you make an offer or inherit a house.

What does a sale do to the next owner's bill?

Ask the title company how the year's tax is divided at the table, and get the balance from the collector, including any certificate. The property appraiser can say what becomes of your exemption.

The buyer should expect a first bill well above yours. A sale resets the parcel to just value on the following January 1.

Frequently asked questions

When does Florida mail property tax bills?

In November, from the county tax collector. The early discount runs 4 percent in November down to 1 percent in February.

Which date makes Florida taxes delinquent?

April 1. Certificates on unpaid accounts are sold by June 1.

Which form claims a homestead exemption?

Form DR-501, filed with the county property appraiser by March 1, for an owner who made the home a permanent residence by January 1.

What is the annual growth limit on homestead value?

The smaller of 3 percent or the CPI change. The Revenue chart shows 2.7 percent for 2026.

How does deferral work for homestead owners?

File DR-570 with the tax collector by March 31 after the assessment year. It covers taxes above 5 percent of household income, or above 3 percent for a permanent resident 65 or older.

What is the Florida homestead exemption worth to an owner?

It shields as much as $50,000 of assessed value from tax, delivered in two layers. Per the state's homestead guide (pt113), the first $25,000 offsets every levy, school taxes included. A further $25,000 applies only to assessed value past the $50,000 mark and skips school taxes.

That second layer moves with inflation. When the CPI change is positive, the amount is adjusted on each January 1; when negative, it holds steady. The department's table starts from a 2024 base, so look at your own bill or ask the appraiser for the amount in force.

The exemption lowers the taxable base and nothing more. Whatever millage the school board, county, city and special districts set still applies to the remainder.

Who qualifies, and what ends the exemption?

Title in your name on January 1, plus permanent residence status by that same day, is the entry ticket. You get one permanent residence at a time.

Three events end it, according to the guide:

  • You rent the unit out.
  • The house stops being your permanent home.
  • You stop being a Florida permanent resident.

Servicemembers have an exception in s. 196.061, which lets them lease the home without abandoning homestead (pt109). Everyone else who relocates should tell the appraiser so a stale exemption does not linger on the roll.

How do I apply, and what if the claim is denied?

Form DR-501 goes to your county appraiser, and the state calendar treats the first of March as the cutoff for exemptions and agricultural classifications (taxpayer calendar).

A denial letter starts a 30 day countdown for a value adjustment board petition. Disputing the value is a separate route: a DR-486 petition filed with the clerk of court within 25 days of the Notice of Proposed Property Taxes, which arrives in August.

Appraisers decide who is eligible and tax collectors mail the bills. When you are unsure which office owns a problem, begin with the appraiser.

What does Save Our Homes do for a long-time owner?

It throttles annual growth in a homestead's assessed value. After the first year, an increase cannot beat the smaller of 3 percent and the CPI change, and assessed value can never pass just value (pt112).

The department's chart, revised in January 2026, lists:

YearCPI changeCap applied
20243.4%3.0%
20252.9%2.9%
20262.7%2.7%

Source: Save Our Homes cap chart. The 2024 row shows the 3 percent ceiling biting while inflation ran higher.

Property without homestead faces a ceiling of 10 percent per year, from the same calendar page.

What happens to the cap when a homestead sells?

The accumulated protection disappears. A sale, foreclosure or any transfer of legal or beneficial title counts as a change of ownership, and the next January 1 the parcel returns to just value. Listed exceptions include spousal transfers and certain transfers at death.

Your exemption stays behind as well. A buyer who moves in applies fresh, and a buyer who rents the place out cannot claim it. The gap between your old bill and the new owner's first full bill can be large for a house held many years.

The tax year of a closing in the spring or summer still carries the assessment fixed the previous January, and the November bill is split under the purchase contract. Read that clause before you sign.

Can I carry my Save Our Homes savings to another house?

Portability allows it when you meet the timing rule. The new homestead must be established within three years counted from January 1 of the year you gave up the old one, not from the closing date. Form DR-501T travels with the DR-501 (pt112).

Statute text lowers the new assessed value by the lesser of $500,000 or the old home's difference between just and assessed value (s. 193.155(8)). The statute page records that ch. 2026-239 amendments first reach the 2027 roll, so ask the appraiser which version governs your move (s. 193.155).

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Are there added breaks for seniors, veterans and disabled owners?

Several, layered on the base exemption, and local governments control some of them.

  • 65 and older: an ordinance may add up to $50,000 where household income stays within the limit, which began at $20,000 and is indexed by CPI (s. 196.075(2)).
  • 65 and older, 25 years a permanent resident, just value below $250,000: an ordinance may exempt the whole assessed value, income limit permitting.
  • Veterans 65 and older with a permanent service-connected disability: a discount equal to the VA disability percentage, which passes to an unremarried surviving spouse (s. 196.082).
  • Disabled former servicemembers rated 10 percent or more: $5,000 off assessed value (ss. 196.081, 196.091).
  • Total and permanent service-connected disability: a possible full exemption on the homestead.

Details are in the state's guides for seniors and veterans. Ask your appraiser which of these your county adopted.

Can homestead tax be deferred?

Part of it can. Form DR-570 reaches the tax collector by March 31 after the assessment year. Deferral covers tax beyond 5 percent of the previous year's household income, or everything when income is under $10,000. Permanent residents 65 and older may defer the slice beyond 3 percent of income.

On payment, the November bill carries a 4 percent discount, December 3, January 2 and February 1. Unpaid amounts go delinquent on April 1 and certificates are sold by June 1 (calendar). A deferral recorded on your home can be cleared with a payoff figure from the tax collector, so request one before listing.

What should a seller with a homestead check before listing?

Open the appraiser's parcel record first. It lists assessed value, just value and exemption status. The distance between those two values is what Save Our Homes has kept off your bill.

  • Confirm the current exemption application was accepted.
  • Note any senior, veteran or disability benefit, since none transfers to a buyer.
  • Find out whether a DR-570 deferral is on record.
  • Decide early whether you intend to port the benefit, because that starts a three year window.

Share the answers with the closing agent so the buyer's own filing can be planned.

It also pays to pull the last two tax bills. Compare the line for each taxing body, because school, county and city rates differ, and a buyer's agent will likely do the same exercise. Seeing which levies the exemption actually reduces tells you whether the buyer's real cost after reassessment is close to yours or far above it. If you recently remodeled, ask the appraiser whether new improvements were added to the roll, since additions can raise just value on their own.

Frequently asked questions

When must a Florida homestead claim be filed?

The first of March, with the county appraiser, using Form DR-501, and you must have made the home your permanent residence by January 1. A denial goes to the value adjustment board, and that petition has a 30 day window running from the mailing of the denial letter.

How big is the Florida homestead exemption?

Up to $50,000 in assessed value. The initial $25,000 offsets all taxes, school levies included. The extra $25,000 touches only value above $50,000 and excludes school taxes. That extra amount is indexed to inflation.

Does a buyer inherit my Save Our Homes cap?

No. Sale means a change of ownership and a return to just value the following January 1. Spouse transfers and certain transfers at death are among the exceptions.

Can I keep my cap savings when I buy elsewhere in Florida?

Often, through portability. Establish the new homestead within three years counted from January 1 of the year you abandoned the old one, and file DR-501T with DR-501. The reduction cannot exceed $500,000 or the old home's just-minus-assessed gap, whichever is lower.

What if I rent my homestead out?

Renting costs you the exemption, as does moving away or leaving Florida as a permanent resident. Servicemembers are the listed exception under s. 196.061.

How do I appeal a property tax assessment in Florida?

You file a sworn petition with the clerk of the county's value adjustment board, known as the VAB, within 25 days of the date the property appraiser mailed the Notice of Proposed Property Taxes. That notice is the TRIM notice, mailed in August.

An informal talk with the appraiser's office is available first, but s. 194.011(2) says it is not a prerequisite to a petition. The 25-day clock keeps running while you talk, so a petition is the safer way to hold your place.

What deadlines apply to a Florida value adjustment board petition?

Two deadlines matter, and they depend on what you dispute. Under s. 194.011(3)(d), valuation issues must be filed on or before the 25th day after the notice is mailed. Denials of an exemption, an agricultural or high-water recharge classification, a historic-property classification or a deferral get 30 days after the mailing of the notice that carries the denial.

  • Valuation dispute: 25 days from the mailed TRIM notice.
  • Exemption, classification or deferral denial: 30 days from the denial notice.
  • VAB hearing evidence: lists and copies exchanged at least 15 days before the hearing.
  • VAB written decision: due within 20 calendar days after the board's last session.
  • Circuit court suit: 60 days from certification of the assessment, or from the board decision in the cases the statute describes.

Who can file or represent me before the board?

The owner can file, or can authorize someone to file. The petition must be signed by the taxpayer or come with written authorization or a power of attorney, and an authorization is valid for only one assessment year. Section 194.034(1) also lists who may appear for a petitioner: an employee of the taxpayer, a Florida Bar attorney, a licensed real estate appraiser or broker, or a certified public accountant retained by the taxpayer, plus an unpaid person holding written authorization.

The petition must name the property by parcel number and state about how much time you expect to need. The property appraiser can also be represented by an attorney, and witnesses on both sides testify under oath if either party asks.

What happens at a Florida VAB hearing?

The board hears the petitioner and the property appraiser, and each side can cross-examine witnesses under Department of Revenue rules. At least 15 days before the hearing, you give the appraiser your list of evidence, copies of documents and a summary of witness testimony, and the appraiser must send you the same, including the property record card. If the appraiser misses that duty, the hearing is rescheduled.

The board may weigh assessments of comparable properties in similar areas. It may not consider evidence the appraiser asked you for in writing and that you withheld. A verbatim record is kept.

What should I gather before filing a Florida value petition?

Collect the TRIM notice, the parcel number and the property record card, which the appraiser must hand you before the hearing. Evidence that tends to matter is evidence of comparable properties in the same neighborhood, since the board may weigh assessments among comparable properties in homogeneous areas.

  • The mailing date printed on the TRIM notice, to count 25 days.
  • Photos or repair estimates if condition is the issue.
  • Recent sales of similar homes nearby.
  • A signed authorization if someone else files for you.

Ask the VAB clerk in your county for the Department of Revenue petition form and the local filing method, because counties differ in how they accept filings.

The petition is sworn, uses the form the Department of Revenue prescribes, and goes to the VAB clerk, who acknowledges receipt and gives the appraiser a copy. A county officer may not refuse the department's form if you choose to use it (s. 194.011(3)). Keep your acknowledgment, since it proves you met the deadline.

What does the board decide, and what comes next?

Except when a petition is withdrawn or the appraiser agrees, the board issues a written decision with findings of fact and conclusions of law, within 20 calendar days after its last session. The clerk mails notice of the result to you and the appraiser, or sends it electronically if you chose that on the petition.

Florida appeal steps by statute
StepRule as printed
File with VAB clerk25 days after notice (value), 30 days after denial notice (exemption or classification)
Exchange evidenceAt least 15 days before hearing
Board decisionWithin 20 calendar days after last session
Circuit court action60 days after certification or board decision

If you disagree with the board, circuit courts have original jurisdiction over property tax matters under s. 194.171, with venue in the county of the property in most cases.

Keep your copy of the decision, because the 60-day court limit can run from the board's ruling in some cases.

What must I pay while contesting an assessment in court?

Before a court action, you must pay the collector at least the tax you admit in good faith to owe, and file the receipt with the complaint (s. 194.171(3)). Paying is not an admission that the tax was correct, and a timely suit suspends collection procedures until the case ends.

Taxes on the same property for later years, to the extent you admit them, must be paid before they become delinquent, or the court loses jurisdiction under s. 194.171(5). These requirements are jurisdictional, so a missed receipt can end the case.

Can neighbors or associations appeal together?

Sometimes. A condominium, cooperative or homeowners' association with board approval may file one joint petition for owners whose units the appraiser finds substantially similar in location, amenities, rooms, living area and condition. The association must notify owners first and give them at least 14 days to opt out in writing.

An owner of contiguous undeveloped parcels, or of several tangible personal property accounts, can also seek a joint petition if the appraiser finds them substantially similar. For tangible personal property, the assessment cannot be contested unless the required return was timely filed (s. 194.034(1)(j)).

What about homestead portability disputes?

If you move a homestead and disagree with the assessment difference carried over, you petition in the county of the new home, and that board notifies the board of the old county, which reconvenes if needed (s. 194.011(6)). You cannot use that proceeding to change the old home's just, assessed or taxable value.

Portability itself requires establishing the new homestead within three years of January 1 of the year the old one was abandoned, with Form DR-501T filed with the DR-501 by March 1.

Frequently asked questions

What is the deadline to appeal my Florida property value?

File with the VAB clerk by the 25th day after the property appraiser mails the Notice of Proposed Property Taxes. A denial of an exemption, classification or deferral carries a 30-day window from the denial notice.

Do I need to meet with the property appraiser first?

No. Section 194.011(2) lets you request an informal conference, but says it is not a prerequisite to administrative or judicial review. The petition deadline keeps running.

Can I hire someone to file for me?

Yes. Section 194.034(1) lists attorneys, licensed appraisers and brokers, CPAs, employees of the taxpayer and persons with written authorization or a power of attorney. The authorization is good for one assessment year and one petitioner.

How long does the board have to decide?

The board must issue its written decision within 20 calendar days after its last day in session under s. 194.032. The clerk then sends notice to you and the property appraiser.

Can I sue in circuit court instead?

You may contest an assessment under s. 194.171 whether or not you filed with the board, but you must pay the tax you admit owing first, and the action must come within 60 days of the dates the statute names.

Florida Tax Deed Sales: Certificates, Redemption and Surplus Funds

Cash Home Buyers in Florida

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Florida Tax Deed Sales sale

Behind on Taxes? Get a Cash Offer Before a Tax Sale

How does a Florida tax deed sale start?

It starts with unpaid property tax. Under the Department of Revenue's taxpayer calendar, the tax collector mails bills in November, taxes turn delinquent on April 1, and the tax collector sells tax certificates on unpaid items by June 1.

A certificate is not a deed. It is a lien the buyer purchases by bidding, and the house stays in the owner's name until a deed is issued after a longer process. A Florida owner who is behind has real time to act, which is the point of this page.

How are tax certificates sold in Florida?

Bidders compete on interest, and the lowest rate wins. Section 197.432 has the tax collector award each certificate to the bidder who demands the lowest rate, in quarter percent steps, and unsold certificates go to the county at the maximum rate.

  • A homestead property with less than $250 delinquent must be issued to the county, not sold at auction.
  • The tax collector keeps a 5 percent commission.
  • The holder may not contact the owner to demand payment until two years after the April 1 that falls in the year of issuance.

Can I pay off a certificate and keep my Florida house?

Yes, at any time after issuance and before a tax deed is issued, as long as the buyer has not yet paid in full for the deed. Section 197.472 has the redeeming person pay the tax collector the face amount plus interest, costs and charges.

When the certificate's earned interest is below 5 percent of face value, a mandatory minimum of 5 percent applies, except on certificates bid at zero percent. The tax collector receives a $6.25 fee per redeemed certificate. A certificate can also be redeemed in part only when the portion can be identified by legal description and is backed by a sale contract or recorded deed. Call the collector about the exact payoff figure for your parcel.

When can the certificate holder apply for a tax deed?

After two years have passed since the April 1 that falls in the year the certificate was issued. Section 197.502 sets an application fee of $75 and has the tax collector list the people who must receive notice: the titleholder, lienholders, mortgagees, contract for deed buyers and the assessed party.

Notice goes to a defined group, so an updated mailing address with the property appraiser and the clerk helps. The clerk's own charge for processing a tax deed application is $60.00 under section 28.24(22).

What does the opening bid include at the auction?

It includes the taxes, interest and costs owed, and for homestead property it also adds one half of the latest assessed value. That is a notable difference from a non-homestead parcel, and the statute page for section 197.502 spells it out.

If nobody bids, the land goes on the list of lands available for taxes. The county then has 90 days to buy it for the opening bid. Three years after the offer, remaining land escheats to the county.

How does the clerk run the sale and collect payment?

The circuit court clerk holds the public auction, and section 197.542 allows electronic sales.

  • The high bidder pays a nonrefundable deposit of 5 percent of the bid or $200, whichever is greater.
  • Full payment, documentary stamps and recording fees are due within 24 hours, excluding weekends and holidays.
  • The certificate holder's bid also earns interest at a monthly rate of 1.5 percent.

To stop the sale, redeem before the winning bidder pays for the deed. After that, the remedy shifts to surplus funds.

Who gets the surplus after a Florida tax deed sale?

Whatever the winning bid exceeds the certificate holder's statutory bid goes into a surplus, and lienholders are paid first. The rules are in section 197.582.

The clerk pays governmental liens of record first, then holds the balance for the people with an interest in the property and mails them a notice. Anyone who gets that notice has 120 days from its date to file a notarized claim with the clerk. A person other than the owner who misses that window is barred from the funds, and if no claim arrives the legal titleholder of record is presumed entitled to the money. Once the claim window closes, the clerk has 90 days to pay by priority or to file an interpleader if claims conflict. Homestead's added opening bid amount is treated as surplus and handled the same way.

What can an owner do in the months after the April 1 delinquency?

Several tools exist before a deed is ever near. The Department of Revenue calendar notes that homestead owners can ask the tax collector about a deferral, filed on Form DR-570 by March 31 after the assessment year, which covers the portion of tax above a share of household income. Owners 65 or older may defer more.

  • Pay in the discount window if you can: the printed schedule runs 4 percent in November, 3 percent in December, 2 percent in January and 1 percent in February.
  • Ask the tax collector about installment prepayment, which needs an application on file by May 1 of the assessment year, per the revenue agency.
  • Call the tax collector about partial payments, which are at that office's discretion before the delinquency date.

These dates matter for next year more than the one already delinquent, so mark them on a calendar.

What happens to the house after the deed sale if the owner stays?

The deed changes who holds title, so the former owner has no right to stay once the buyer takes over. A person living in the house after the deed is in the same position as an unwanted occupant, and the buyer would use the court process or the sheriff route that fits the facts.

For an owner this is the strongest reason to act while the certificate is still outstanding. Redeeming costs the face amount plus interest and fees, and the house remains in the family. Selling to a buyer who closes quickly can pay the certificate through the title company, which treats the tax collector's payoff as one more lien to clear.

Heirs who inherit a house with a certificate on it should call the tax collector first. Ask which certificates exist, their issue dates and whether an application for a deed has been filed. The clerk can say whether a sale date is set, and the property appraiser can confirm who is listed as owner. Bring a death certificate or letters after an owner passes away, because the notice list is built from the names on record and a missed notice can affect the sale.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What does each stage cost and when does it happen?

StageTiming or amount
Taxes delinquentApril 1
Certificate soldBy June 1
RedemptionBefore deed issued; 5 percent minimum interest
Deed applicationAfter 2 years from April 1 of issuance; $75
Auction deposit5 percent or $200, balance in 24 hours
Surplus claim120 days from notice

Should I sell the house before a tax deed sale?

A sale ahead of the auction lets the title company pay tax and certificate charges at closing and may leave something for the owner. The payoff amount comes from the tax collector, so request it in writing before you choose a buyer.

Compare that with waiting: after a deed sale, the owner's recovery depends on a surplus that exists only if the bidding exceeds what is owed, and every lienholder is paid ahead of the former owner.

Frequently asked questions

Can an owner halt a Florida tax deed auction?

Yes, by redeeming the certificate before the deed is paid for. You pay the tax collector the face amount plus interest, costs and charges, and interest is at least 5 percent unless the certificate was bid at zero.

When can the county sale of the house happen?

The holder can apply for a deed after two years from the April 1 that falls in the year the certificate was issued. The clerk then runs the auction.

What happens if no one bids at the auction?

The land goes on the lands available for taxes list. The county has 90 days to buy it for the opening bid, and three years after the offer the land escheats to the county.

Do I get money back if the house sells high?

Possibly. A surplus is paid to lienholders first, and the titleholder is presumed entitled to what remains when no other claim arrives within 120 days. Ask the clerk about your file.

Does homestead status change the auction?

Yes. The opening bid on homestead includes one half of the latest assessed value, and small delinquencies under $250 on homestead cannot be auctioned as certificates.

Compensation questions go to the listing contract.

Does Florida law set a real estate commission rate?

No Florida statute sets a commission rate for selling a home. The fee is whatever the seller and the listing broker agree to in writing, and it can be negotiated.

What state law does regulate is the paperwork around that fee. The licensing statutes say what a listing agreement must contain, which relationships a licensee may have with a client, and who may be paid for real estate services at all. That is where a seller's protections sit, so it is worth knowing the outline before signing anything.

What must a Florida listing agreement include?

Under s. 475.25(1)(r), a licensee can be disciplined for a written listing agreement that leaves out any of these items:

  • a definite expiration date;
  • a description of the property;
  • the price and terms;
  • the fee or commission;
  • the signature of the principal or principals.

The same paragraph requires the broker to give the seller a legible, signed, true and correct copy within 24 hours of obtaining the signed agreement. It also says the agreement may not require the seller to give notice of an intention to cancel after the expiration date has passed. In plain terms, a Florida listing is supposed to end on the date written in it, with no automatic renewal that you must cancel.

Read the fee line twice. Because the statute leaves the rate to the parties, the number in your agreement is the number that governs, along with any tail period or bonus the contract adds.

What should a seller compare before choosing a listing broker?

Because the statute leaves price to the parties, two brokers can quote different fees for the same house, and the number is only part of the comparison. Put each proposal side by side and ask about the following.

  • The expiration date and whether the broker will release the listing early if the house does not sell.
  • Whether the broker will serve as your single agent or as a transaction broker, in writing.
  • How and where the broker holds deposits. Florida requires brokers to place entrusted money in escrow with a title company or bank, or in the broker's own trust account, as soon as it is received.
  • What the fee covers, and whether any amount is owed if you later sell to a buyer you found yourself.

A seller who is also weighing an as-is cash offer should set that offer next to the net from a listing, after the fee, repairs, carrying costs and the time the house sits on the market. The numbers belong in writing on both sides.

Can a seller avoid paying a commission in Florida?

Yes, if no licensed agent is hired. Section 475.011(2) exempts an individual or company that sells, exchanges or leases its own real property from the licensing part of the chapter, so a homeowner selling a house can do it without a license and without a broker's fee (s. 475.011).

That exemption covers the owner. It does not let the owner pay an unlicensed helper for finding buyers. The licensing law prohibits a licensee from sharing a commission or paying other compensation to anyone who is not properly licensed for referring business or performing the services in s. 475.01(1)(a). An owner who wants help on commission should hire a licensed broker.

The exemption also contains a limit: it is not available when a salesperson is paid a commission or other compensation strictly on a transactional basis to make sales for an owner who is in the business of selling property to the public. A homeowner with a single house is outside that carve-out.

What relationships can a Florida agent have with a seller?

A licensee may work as a single agent or as a transaction broker, and may not act as a dual agent (s. 475.278). The statute presumes transaction brokerage unless a single-agent relationship, or no relationship, is set up in writing.

The duties differ, and the difference matters to anyone paying a commission.

RelationshipDuties the statute lists
Single agentHonesty and fair dealing, loyalty, confidentiality, obedience, full disclosure, accounting for funds, skill and care, presenting offers, disclosing known material facts
Transaction brokerHonesty and fair dealing, accounting for funds, skill and care, presenting offers, disclosing known material facts, limited confidentiality
No brokerage relationshipHonesty and fair dealing, disclosing known material facts, accounting for entrusted funds

Source: Fla. Stat. s. 475.278. A single agent owes the seller loyalty, which a transaction broker does not. The statute describes a transaction broker as giving a limited form of representation, so a seller who wants an agent pushing for the highest price should ask for single-agent status in writing.

How does the written disclosure work?

A single agent must describe those duties in writing, either in a separate document or inside the listing agreement. The statute requires the disclosure before or at the time the listing agreement or agreement for representation is signed, or before showing the property, whichever comes first.

When the notice sits inside another document it has to be in type at least as large as the rest and placed conspicuously, with the first sentence in uppercase bold. A licensee who switches from single agent to transaction broker must first obtain the seller's written consent.

These rules apply to residential sales, defined as improved residential property of four units or fewer, unimproved land intended for four units or fewer, or agricultural property of 10 acres or fewer. Nonresidential deals, auctions and appraisals fall outside them.
