What protections does a seller have if a broker misbehaves?

The same section that governs listing agreements lets the state discipline a licensee for a long list of conduct. Penalties in s. 475.25(1) include probation, suspension for up to 10 years, revocation, a reprimand, and an administrative fine of up to $5,000 for each count or separate offense.

A few of the listed grounds matter directly to a home seller:

  • failing to account for or deliver money, deposits or documents that belong to someone else;
  • failing to place a deposit in escrow with a Florida title company or bank, or in the broker's own trust account, immediately on receipt;
  • fraud, misrepresentation, concealment or breach of trust in a transaction;
  • deceptive advertising of property or services;
  • giving an opinion that title is good without a current attorney's opinion, or without advising the buyer to consult an attorney or obtain title insurance.

An administrative complaint must be filed within 5 years after the act, or within 5 years after the act was or should have been discovered with due diligence. Keep your signed listing agreement, the disclosure of the agent's duties and your closing statement for that long.

What other fees come out of a Florida sale?

The commission is one line among several. Sellers should ask the closing agent for a written estimate of each before listing.

  • Documentary stamp tax on the deed: the statute sets 70 cents per $100 of consideration,.
  • Clerk recording charges on the deed and any release of an old mortgage.
  • Payoff of any mortgage, liens or unpaid property taxes.
  • Prorated property taxes for the part of the year you owned the house.

A cash buyer who purchases as-is can remove the agent commission line from this list, since no broker is involved, though the tax and recording items remain. Compare offers by what you would net after every line, and ask each buyer to put its terms in writing.

Frequently asked questions

Is the commission fixed by Florida law?

No. Florida statutes do not set a rate, so the fee comes from the listing agreement you sign and can be negotiated before signing.

Can a Florida listing agreement renew automatically?

The statute requires a definite expiration date and says the agreement may not require the seller to give notice to cancel after that date, so a listing should lapse on its stated date.

Do I need a license to sell my own house in Florida?

No. Section 475.011(2) exempts an owner who sells their own real property from the licensing part of the chapter.

Can a Florida agent act for both buyer and seller?

A licensee may not act as a dual agent. The statute does allow transaction brokerage, a limited form of representation that does not carry fiduciary duties.

How soon must I get a copy of my listing agreement?

Within 24 hours. Section 475.25(1)(r) requires the broker to give the seller a signed, legible, true and correct copy within that window.

Does a Florida homeowner owe tax on profit from selling a house?

Possibly, but a federal exclusion wipes out most or all of the profit for many sellers of a main residence. A single filer can shield $250,000 of profit, and a married couple filing together can shield $500,000, as long as two tests are passed. The figure applies to a Florida house exactly as it would to a house anywhere else in the country.

What Florida adds is local paperwork around the transfer: the deed, the stamp tax collected at recording, and the county's reassessment of the property for the next owner. Those pieces are covered after the federal rules below.

Which two tests unlock the exclusion?

You need to pass an ownership test and a use test inside the five years that end on the closing date. Each test asks for 24 months, and the months need not be consecutive. The IRS also says the two tests may be satisfied in different two-year stretches, provided both land in that five-year window.

  • Ownership: you or your spouse held title for two years out of the five.
  • Use: the house was your residence for two years out of the five, and on a joint return both spouses must pass this one.
  • Prior sale: the break is generally unavailable if you claimed it on a different house during the two years before this closing.

Publication 523, the IRS guide to selling a home, has the worksheets, the partial exclusions for early moves, and the exceptions to the two-year rule. Read it before you assume that eighteen months is enough.

How is the taxable profit figured when the exclusion falls short?

Take the price you realize at closing and subtract your adjusted basis. Basis starts with your cost and rises with permanent improvements such as a new roof or an added bedroom. It falls with items like depreciation and insurance payments for casualty losses. Hold on to old closing statements and contractor receipts, because they are your proof.

Holding period decides the label. Profit on property you held longer than a year is long-term and eligible for the lower rate bands. Anything held a year or less is short-term and is taxed like wages. If the house came to you by inheritance or gift, the IRS sends you to Publication 551 for basis, which matters to a Florida family clearing out a relative's home.

A loss on a personal residence cannot be deducted. Losses on investment property are different: they offset gains, and up to $3,000 of any excess ($1,500 for married filing separately) reduces other income each year, with the balance carried forward.

What federal rates apply to profit above the exclusion?

Most net long-term gain falls into a 0%, 15% or 20% band set by taxable income, and the IRS prints different bands for each filing status. The table copies the bands the IRS shows for tax years starting in 2025. Thresholds move annually, so look at the IRS page for the year of your closing.

IRS long-term gain bands for tax years beginning in 2025

0%Income up to $48,350Income up to $96,700
15%$48,350 to $533,400$96,700 to $600,050
20%Income above the 15% bandIncome above the 15% band

Two extra items can raise the bill. A 25% ceiling applies to the unrecaptured section 1250 slice of gain, which arises when depreciation was claimed on a home office or rental space. Sellers with large investment income may also face a separate surtax that the IRS describes on Topic 559.

Must a fully excluded sale still go on the return?

It must if the closing agent sends you a Form 1099-S. The IRS says to report the sale in that case even though no tax results. If the gain is larger than your exclusion, report it too, on the Form 8949 and Schedule D pair that the IRS names for this.

Keep a folder for the sale: the purchase closing statement, improvement receipts, the new settlement statement and any 1099-S. A tax preparer can work from those papers in minutes, and a missing receipt can leave a legitimate improvement out of your basis.

Title companies in Florida normally prepare the 1099-S from the settlement statement. Ask your closing agent before you sign whether one will be filed in your name. Sellers with a taxable gain may also owe estimated payments during the year, which Publication 505 explains.

Are there timing rules for military sellers and installment sales?

Yes. A service member, Foreign Service officer or intelligence community employee on qualified extended duty may elect to freeze the five-year clock for as long as ten years. Extended duty means more than 90 days or an open-ended assignment, at a post 50 or more miles from the home or in government quarters under orders. Many Florida owners near bases and ports fit this description.

A sale where the buyer pays across later years counts as an installment sale, and the IRS tells sellers to use installment reporting unless they opt out. The home sale exclusion still applies to the part you can exclude. Look at Publication 537 and Form 6252 for the mechanics.

What Florida deed and reassessment rules touch the sale?

Florida taxes the deed at seventy cents on each $100 of price in every county except Miami-Dade, where the printed charge is 60 cents plus a surtax. That surtax is skipped for a paper conveying only a single-family dwelling. Every party to the deed is liable, whoever the contract says will pay. The clerk takes payment when the deed goes on record.

  • An estate's personal representative who deeds property under a probated will is listed as not taxable.
  • A spousal homestead deed whose only consideration is a mortgage is exempt, and so is a divorce deed for the marital home.
  • One Department advisement found a lady bird deed outside the stamp tax on the facts it described, so ask a Florida attorney before relying on that.

For the buyer, the new owner's assessment resets to full just value, ending the old Save Our Homes cap. Florida also hands residential buyers a written tax disclosure, which tells them not to assume your current bill will carry over. A homestead owner who plans to buy again should look at portability, which the Department says requires the new homestead to be established inside a three-year window that is counted from the year the old homestead was abandoned, with Form DR-501T filed alongside the DR-501 by March 1. These steps change the buyer's cost, not your gain.

Frequently asked questions

Does the federal exclusion work the same way for a Florida home?

Yes. The $250,000 and $500,000 limits come from federal tax law and apply to a main home anywhere in the country. Florida does not change the ownership and use tests, though the deed and county records follow Florida procedure.

How many months must I live in the house before selling?

Twenty-four months of residence and twenty-four months of ownership, both inside the five years ending at closing. The months need not be consecutive, and the two tests may be met in different two-year periods.

Can I take the exclusion again soon after another sale?

Generally not. The IRS says you usually cannot if you excluded profit on another house during the two years before this closing. Publication 523 lists exceptions.

I will owe nothing. Do I still tell the IRS?

If a Form 1099-S arrives, yes. The IRS wants it reported even if every dollar of gain is excludable, and also when part of the gain is taxable.

What counts toward my basis?

Your purchase cost plus lasting improvements, reduced by depreciation and insurance reimbursements for casualty losses. Inherited or gifted homes follow different basis rules in IRS Publication 551.

A 1031 exchange requires you to identify replacement property within 45 days and receive it within 180 days, and only real property held for business or investment qualifies. These are IRS rules, not Florida rules.

Selling a house in Florida?

What is a 1031 exchange for a Florida property owner?

A 1031 exchange lets an investor who sells real property and buys replacement real property report the swap on Form 8824 instead of reporting a taxable sale. The IRS instructions for that form say the rules now reach exchanges of real property only, and the property must be held for business or investment rather than lived in as a main home. A Florida rental house, a small apartment building or vacant land held as an investment can all be the "given up" property, and the replacement does not have to sit in Florida.

The exchange is a federal tax matter. Florida adds its own paperwork, mainly the deed and the county clerk's recording of it, which are covered further down this page. Anyone who lives in the house they are selling should read the home sale exclusion page for the main residence rules, since that tax break works differently.

What are the 45-day and 180-day deadlines?

You must name the replacement property in writing within 45 days after you transfer the property you give up, and you must receive it by the earlier of 180 days after that transfer or the due date, with extensions, of your tax return for that year. Both clocks start on the closing date of the sale, and the IRS instructions give no extra time for weekends or holidays.

The written identification has to describe the replacement in a clear and recognizable way. For real estate, the instructions accept a legal description, a street address or a distinguishable name such as the name of an apartment building. The signed document must reach the person who is to transfer the replacement property to you, or another person involved in the exchange who is not a disqualified person, before the 45th day ends. Alternatively, every party can sign one written agreement naming the property by that date.

  • Day 0: closing on the Florida property you are giving up.
  • Day 45: last day to identify replacement property in writing.
  • Day 180, or the return due date with extensions if sooner: last day to receive the replacement.

Because the 180-day period can be cut short by the return due date, an owner who closes late in a year should ask a tax professional whether to extend the return so the full period stays available.

Do you need a qualified intermediary in Florida?

In a deferred exchange, where the sale and the purchase close on different days, using a qualified intermediary is the common structure, and the IRS says an exchange run through one is still treated as a like-kind exchange. The seller never takes hold of the sale money. The intermediary holds it and uses it to buy the replacement property.

The Form 8824 instructions warn that if you miss the timing rules because of the intermediary, the deal can fail as a deferred exchange and the gain may be taxable in the year you transferred the property. They also describe a qualified exchange accommodation arrangement for cases where the replacement is acquired first. Ask the intermediary how it protects your funds and what happens if a deadline is missed, and read the exchange agreement before you sign it.

Which Florida properties qualify and which do not?

Real property held for investment or business use qualifies, and personal property such as furniture or equipment no longer does. Your own home does not qualify as the property given up. The IRS instructions include a section on property used as a home and on property used partly as a home, so a duplex where you live in one unit needs a careful split.

  • Likely to qualify: a rented single-family house, a small multifamily building, commercial space, farmland or raw land held for investment.
  • Unlikely to qualify: your main residence, a home held for quick resale as inventory, or a condo you use as a vacation home.
  • Needs advice: a property you rented out but also stayed in, since the use mix drives the answer.

The instructions also say incidental personal property that goes with the real estate is acceptable only within a 15 percent limit of the replacement property's fair market value. Furnished rentals are worth raising with the tax adviser before you list.

What happens if you swap with a relative or related company?

Special rules apply, and an exchange built to avoid them is treated as a sale. The IRS defines a related party to include your spouse, child, grandchild, parent, grandparent, brother or sister, and certain related corporations, partnerships, trusts, estates and tax-exempt organizations. The rule also reaches a swap made through an intermediary, and a swap made by a single-member LLC that you or a related party owned.

If you do a related-party exchange, you must file Form 8824 for the year of the exchange and for the two years after it. Florida investors who keep property in family LLCs should list every owner before they pick a replacement, because a swap with a related party on the other side can change the tax result.

What Florida closing items still apply to a 1031 sale?

The Florida deed is taxed like any other sale deed. The Department of Revenue says the documentary stamp tax on a deed is 70 cents per $100 of consideration in every county except Miami-Dade, where the printed rate is 60 cents plus a surtax that does not apply to a document that transfers only a single-family dwelling. All parties to the document are liable for the tax, even though the contract decides who pays it.

The deed is recorded with the clerk of the circuit court, and the recording fee schedule in section 28.24 of the Florida Statutes sets the page charges. A deed also has to be signed in front of two witnesses under section 689.01. For the tax side of the closing, the Department of Revenue's documentary stamp page lists which deeds are taxable.

Key rules for a Florida 1031 exchange
ItemRule as printed by the source
Identify replacementIn writing within 45 days after transfer (IRS Form 8824 instructions)
Receive replacementEarlier of 180 days or return due date with extensions (IRS)
Property typeReal property only after the regulations (IRS)
Related partyFile Form 8824 for the exchange year and two years after (IRS)
Deed stamp tax70 cents per $100 outside Miami-Dade (Florida Department of Revenue)

Ask your Florida title agent or closing attorney how the intermediary will receive funds, since the exchange paperwork has to be in place before the sale closes.

Frequently asked questions

Can I do a 1031 exchange on my Florida home?

Not on a main residence. The IRS rules apply to real property held for business or investment, and the Form 8824 instructions give separate treatment to property used as a home. If you lived in the house, look at the home sale exclusion instead and ask a tax professional about any rental period.

Is there any extension of the 45-day or 180-day deadline?

The 180-day period ends early if your tax return is due sooner, and an extension of the return can keep the full period open. The IRS instructions describe no extra days for weekends or holidays, so count calendar days from the closing.

Does Florida require a separate form for a 1031 exchange?

Ask the clerk or your title agent if any county form applies. You report the exchange on federal Form 8824 with your return, and the deed and its stamp tax follow the usual Florida closing steps through the clerk of the circuit court.

Do I pay documentary stamp tax when I sell the old property?

Yes, the deed is taxable. The Department of Revenue lists warranty, special warranty and quitclaim deeds among taxable documents, and all parties are liable for the tax even if the contract assigns it to one side. Ask your closing agent which party pays under your contract.

Can I buy replacement property in another state?

The IRS instructions do not tie replacement property to Florida. They speak of like-kind real property and ask filers to note the country when real property is outside the United States. Confirm the details of an out-of-state purchase with your intermediary.

What does the Census Bureau report on Florida housing?

Florida counted 10,789,047 housing units on July 1, 2025, alongside an estimated 23,462,518 residents, and the middle owner-reported home value is $359,000 in the 2020 to 2024 data.

Growth is brisk. Growth since April 2020 is 8.9 percent. Population per square mile climbed from 350.6 to 401.4 between 2010 and 2020, over 53,652.17 square miles of land. New supply keeps arriving too, with 178,297 building permits recorded for 2025.

What share of Florida households own their homes?

About two of every three homes: 67.6 percent in the 2020 to 2024 data. That leaves about a third of occupied homes to renters. The bureau counts 8,752,810 households averaging 2.51 people.

Residents mostly stay put. About 86.3 percent of people aged one and older had not moved in the prior year. Sellers therefore draw buyers from arrivals as much as from neighbors trading up.

The age mix is notable. Those 65 and older make up 22.8 percent of the population, and 1,327,071 residents are veterans. Both groups connect to homestead benefits described in the state's senior and veteran guides, which shape what a buyer or an heir pays after a sale.

What are typical monthly housing costs in Florida?

Median monthly cost runs $1,959 for owners still paying a mortgage and $673 for owners who are not. Renters face $1,669 in gross rent. The bureau labels all three as 2020 to 2024 estimates.

The spread between the owner figures shows how much of a payment is the loan itself. A paid-off house still carries taxes, insurance and upkeep, so an heir holding a free-and-clear property pays less per month yet faces vacancy risk, repairs and the autumn tax bill.

For comparison, median household income is $74,568 in 2024 dollars, per capita income is $42,609, and 12.0 percent of people are below the poverty line.

How does homestead protection split buyers from long-time owners?

It opens a gap. Save Our Homes holds a homestead's assessed value growth to the smaller of 3 percent or CPI, and a sale resets the parcel to just value the next January 1 (pt112). Property without homestead is limited to 10 percent per year, which explains why neighboring houses can carry quite different bills.

  • Read the appraiser's record for assessed and just value.
  • Ask the tax collector about any deferral or installment plan.
  • Check that an owner who moved out has not left a stale exemption.

None of that shows up in a median, so local records beat averages.

Which county offices does a Florida seller deal with?

Florida is divided into 67 counties, and each elects a sheriff, tax collector, property appraiser, supervisor of elections and clerk of the circuit court to four year terms (Senate bill analysis). Three of those offices touch a home sale.

  • The property appraiser sets just value each January, mails the August notice and rules on exemptions.
  • The tax collector bills, collects, takes deferral and installment requests, and sells certificates on unpaid items.
  • The clerk of the circuit court records the deed, takes the stamp tax and runs foreclosure and tax deed auctions.

Knowing which door to knock on saves a seller days at closing.

What happens to unpaid Florida property tax?

Unpaid tax turns delinquent on April 1, and the tax collector sells certificates on unpaid items by June 1 (state calendar). Bidders compete on the lowest interest rate in quarter percent steps, and the county takes any certificate that finds no bidder at the maximum rate (s. 197.432).

A certificate holder may not demand payment from the owner until two years after April 1 of the issue year, and may apply for a tax deed after that same period. Homeowners considering a quick sale should clear delinquencies first, since a buyer's lender will insist.

What should a seller verify before leaning on statewide averages?

Look at the county, the neighborhood and the house. One state median blends beach condos, inland ranch homes and rural parcels.

County offices hold the facts that set closing costs. The appraiser publishes values, the clerk records deeds and collects stamp tax, and the tax collector sends bills.

QuickFacts does not carry sale price, days on market or sales volume. A local agent or the clerk's recorded sales can fill that gap.

What questions should a Florida seller ask a local office?

Write the questions down before calling, because each office answers only its own slice. Useful ones include the following.

  • To the appraiser: what are the current assessed and just values, and is every exemption still active?
  • To the tax collector: are any taxes, deferrals or installment plans open against the parcel?
  • To the clerk: how will the deed be recorded, and what stamp tax and recording charges will apply?

Answers vary by county, and a house in a high-growth county may be assessed very differently from a similar one inland. Use the statewide Census figures here as a backdrop, then replace them with the county and city rows when you set a price or plan repairs.

Closing agents can estimate the settlement figures once they see the contract, so request a draft statement early rather than the week of closing.

What share of Florida homes are owner-occupied?

67.6 percent for 2020 to 2024. The state has 8,752,810 households averaging 2.51 people.

What does a Florida renter pay?

A median gross rent of $1,669 in the 2020 to 2024 data. Owner costs are $1,959 a month with a mortgage and $673 without.

How many homes does Florida have?

10,789,047 housing units on July 1, 2025, for a population estimated at 23,462,518.

Do Florida sellers face a deed tax?

Yes, documentary stamp tax at 70 cents per $100 of consideration in most counties. Miami-Dade charges 60 cents plus a 45 cent surtax that a single-family dwelling transfer avoids. The state holds all parties liable.

Where do Florida deeds and mortgages get filed for public view?

Each of the 67 counties keeps its own Official Records, run by the county clerk. A deed, mortgage or lien filed there becomes searchable by anyone, and the clerk takes the stamp tax due on a deed at the counter.

No single statewide index exists. To look up a parcel, search the Official Records of the county where it lies, then check the appraiser's website for owner name, parcel number and assessed value.

Why does filing a deed matter to the buyer?

An unfiled deed leaves the buyer exposed. Section 695.01 says a conveyance, transfer or mortgage of real property, or a lease running a year or more, is ineffective against creditors and later good-faith purchasers who lack notice unless it is filed as the law requires.

The same section deems a quitclaim grantee a purchaser without notice under the recording acts. It also says a lien from a government or quasi-government body for an improvement, service, fine or penalty binds later purchasers only when recorded, with tax, special assessment and utility liens carved out.

The rule also reaches agents. A deed or mortgage signed under a power of attorney is not effective against creditors or later purchasers unless the power of attorney was itself recorded before their rights arose. Anyone selling a house for an owner who cannot sign should record the power of attorney first.

What formatting does a Florida clerk check before accepting a document?

Section 695.26 lists layout rules, and a deed that breaks them can be bounced at the counter, which delays a closing.

  • Every signer's name typed or printed under the signature, with a mailing address.
  • Who prepared the paper, with a mailing address.
  • Printed names and addresses for each witness.
  • A printed name under any notary's signature.
  • Blank margin boxes at the top right: 3 by 3 inches on page one, 1 by 3 inches on later pages.
  • Each grantee's name and mailing address, except on a mortgage.

Wills, plats, court orders, papers signed by public officers, instruments from before July 1, 1991 and those signed outside the state are exempt from these rules. If the clerk takes a nonconforming page anyway, the recording still stands.

Does a Florida deed need witnesses?

Yes, two. Section 689.01 requires a written conveyance of a freehold or of a term over one year to be signed with two subscribing witnesses present. A seal is not required, and the witnessing can take place by audio-video technology.

That requirement covers quitclaim and lady bird deeds as well. A missing witness can lead a title insurer to refuse the document later.

What are the clerk's per-page fees?

Two kinds of charge show up on a closing statement: the clerk's page fees and stamp tax. The first group comes from s. 28.24.

Clerk charges printed in s. 28.24 for instruments up to 14 by 8.5 inches

Page count and the number of names drive the total, so ask the clerk's recording desk for a figure on your actual document.

How is stamp tax figured on a Florida deed?

Section 201.02(1)(a) puts the deed rate at 70 cents on each $100 of consideration. Consideration covers cash, a released obligation and any mortgage or encumbrance on the land, whether the buyer assumes it or not.

Miami-Dade follows a different formula on the Revenue page: 60 cents per $100 plus a 45 cents per $100 surtax, and the surtax is not due when the paper moves only a single-family home. Every other county uses 70 cents per $100 or portion thereof.

  • Every party to the paper is liable, whoever agrees to pay.
  • Unrecorded taxable paper goes to the state revenue agency rather than the clerk.
  • Taxable deeds named by Revenue include warranty, special warranty, quit claim, trustee's, life estate, contract for deed, deed in lieu and certificate of title.
  • Mortgages and notes bear 35 cents per $100 secured; the note tax stops at $2,450.

Which transfers are treated differently?

Revenue lists a deed from an estate's fiduciary under a probated will as not taxable. A homestead deed between spouses where the only consideration is a mortgage, and a divorce deed for the marital home, are exempt under s. 201.02(7).

Revenue also says no specific exemption exists for estate-planning transfers. Advisement TAA 20B4-004 (October 2020) found a lady bird deed on its particular facts passed no present beneficial interest, so it escaped the tax, though other facts could change the answer.

Any transfer of title also counts as a change of ownership for Save Our Homes unless an exception fits, which resets the next January 1 assessment to just value. Check with the property appraiser before deeding a long-held homestead.

Which county offices hold which pieces of the property file?

A parcel's paper trail is split between three elected offices. The clerk holds recorded instruments and takes deed stamp tax, the property appraiser sets just value each January 1 and rules on exemptions, and the tax collector bills and collects.

  • Clerk: deeds, mortgages, liens, tax deed and foreclosure sale paperwork.
  • Property appraiser: ownership on the roll, TRIM notice and exemption decisions.
  • Tax collector: November bills, delinquency, tax certificates.

Plat filings carry their own clerk charge in s. 28.24: $30.00 for the first page and $15.00 for each additional page. A surveyor or developer subdividing land should budget for that separately from deed recording.

What shows up after a foreclosure or tax deed sale?

Mortgages and liens appear in a title search and need payoff or release before a clean deed can pass. A foreclosure sale ends in a certificate of title, on which tax is figured from the highest and best bid under s. 201.02(9).

A tax deed buyer owes stamp tax and recording fees within 24 hours of the auction, excluding weekends and holidays. A recorded contract-for-deed vendee is among the parties the tax collector lists for notice before that sale, which shows how recording protects an installment buyer.

How should a seller review the records before listing?

Pull the vesting deed, each recorded mortgage and any lien. That tells you what must be paid off at closing and whether the name on title matches the person signing.

If title came through an estate, a gift or an unusual deed, ask the recording desk what it will accept before you schedule a closing date.

Also note any government lien for a fine or penalty. Under s. 695.01(3), such a lien is valid against later buyers only if the notice of lien was recorded and shows the owner of record, a description or address and the parcel number, so a recorded notice on your parcel is worth reading line by line before you sign a listing agreement.

Frequently asked questions

Which office takes deeds for recording in Florida?

The clerk in the county where the land lies. That office also collects stamp tax on the deed when it is filed, so bring a document that meets the form rules.

What changes the recording bill?

Page count and extra names. Section 28.24(13) prints $5.00 for page one, $4.00 for later pages and $1.00 per name beyond four, plus trust fund and technology charges. The clerk can quote the sum.

Is the stamp rate identical in all 67 counties?

Nearly. Miami-Dade is listed at 60 cents per $100 plus a 45 cents surtax that skips single-family transfers, while the rest use 70 cents per $100.

Is an unfiled deed worthless?

Not between the signers, but s. 695.01 withholds effect against creditors and later buyers for value without notice. Stamp tax is also owed on deeds recorded or not.

Do the layout rules reach every instrument?

No. Wills, plats, court orders, papers signed by public officers and instruments signed outside Florida are exempt, and a clerk may accept a page whose name placement is odd if the signer link is plain.

When a Florida rental property is sold, all security deposits and advance rents held for tenants must be transferred to the new owner or the buyer must be told to assume them. A landlord cannot use self-help to remove a tenant.

Selling a house in Florida?
Get My Cash Offer →

What must a landlord do with tenant money when selling a rented house in Florida?

Section 83.49(7) requires the seller to hand all security deposits and advance rents to the new owner, with earned interest and an accurate accounting for each tenant account. The transfer is the landlord's job at the time of sale, so build it into the closing checklist.

Once the funds and records move and the new owner or agent signs a written receipt, the seller is released from the duty to hold that money. A new owner is presumed to have received the deposit from the previous owner, but that presumption stops at one month's rent. A buyer who skips the transfer can end up facing a tenant's refund claim for money it never saw.

Deposits have their own rules while held. The landlord keeps the money in a Florida account for the tenant's benefit, or posts a surety bond with the circuit court clerk, and must give written notice of how it is held within 30 days of receiving it. Landlords renting fewer than five units are excused from that notice, though not from holding the funds properly.

Timing at move-out matters too. A landlord making no claim must refund the deposit inside 15 days of the tenancy's end. One who wants to keep part must send a written claim by certified mail or e-mail inside 30 days, and the tenant gets 15 days to object. A buyer who inherits a tenancy inherits these clocks, so ask the seller for the full ledger.

  • Each tenant's deposit and advance rent amount.
  • Where the money is held and any interest earned.
  • The date each lease began and any renewal, since a renewal counts as a new rental agreement and carries the deposit forward as new.
  • A copy of each signed lease and the written notice that told the tenant how the deposit is held.
  • The name and mailing address of whoever will take over notices and rent after closing.

Can a tenant be forced out so the house can be sold empty?

Only through the notices and court steps in Chapter 83. The statute does not list a planned sale as a reason to end a lease early, so read the lease term first and match it to the right notice period.

Section 83.57 sets the notice to end a periodic tenancy, measured before the end of the rental period.

  • Monthly tenancy: 30 days or more.
  • Yearly tenancy: 60 days or more.
  • Quarterly tenancy: 30 days or more.
  • Weekly tenancy: 7 days or more.

A tenant with a fixed-term lease generally stays through the term unless the lease or the statute provides a ground to end it. Have a Florida landlord-tenant attorney read the lease before any buyer is told the keys will be handed over empty.

What notices apply if the tenant is behind or breaking the lease?

Nonpayment gets a 3-day notice under section 83.56(3), counted without Saturdays, Sundays or court-observed holidays. The notice demands the rent or possession.

Other violations are split into two kinds. For a curable violation, the tenant has 7 days after delivery to fix it. For an incurable one, such as intentional damage to the property or continued unreasonable disturbance, the notice gives 7 days to vacate. A repeat of the same violation within 12 months lets the landlord sue without new notice.

Delivery can be by mail, handing over a true copy, e-mail under section 83.505, or leaving a copy at the residence when the tenant is absent. A lease cannot waive these notice requirements. If the landlord accepts partial rent after serving a 3-day notice, the landlord must give a receipt with the balance due, pay that rent into the court registry when filing, or serve a new notice.

What happens in court after a notice runs out?

Suit is filed, the tenant gets a short window to pay rent into the registry, and a sheriff carries out any judgment.

Under section 83.60(2), a tenant who raises any defense other than payment must pay accrued rent into the court registry, or file a motion to determine rent, within 5 days after service, again excluding Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays. A tenant who misses that step waives the defenses and the landlord gets an immediate default judgment.

After judgment, the clerk issues a writ to the sheriff, who puts the landlord back in possession after 24 hours' conspicuously posted notice. Under section 83.62 weekends and holidays do not stop that 24-hour clock. Build the listing timeline around these steps, because each one adds days.

What does the landlord owe the tenant before and after the sale?

Chapter 83 has the landlord identify, in writing and by the first day of the tenancy, who the landlord or the authorized notice recipient is, with a street address. Section 83.50 says that person keeps the authority until the tenant is told otherwise.

After a sale, tenants need to know where to send rent and notices. Have the closing attorney draft a written notice naming the new owner or agent, delivered to the tenant's residence or by e-mail under section 83.505.

What taxes and costs should a landlord-seller expect?

A landlord-seller pays the same deed tax as any seller, and the rental status changes how the property tax bill behaves. Section 201.02 sets deed tax at 70 cents per $100, collected by the clerk when the deed is recorded.

Rental property has no homestead protection, so the tax cap on a primary home does not help it. Its assessed value is limited to a 10 percent annual increase, and the buyer starts at just value after the transfer. The tax collector mails bills in November, and the state calendar lists early-payment discounts that shrink each month through February.

A house that was once the owner's home and is now rented has lost its exemption, because renting ends homestead. Ask the county property appraiser to confirm the roll, and ask the tax collector for the payoff figure before closing day. A buyer's lender will want that number early.

Frequently asked questions

What happens to my tenant's security deposit when I sell?

Transfer it. Section 83.49(7) requires the seller to pass the deposits and advance rents to the new owner with earned interest and an accounting for each tenant. Get a written receipt, and the seller is released from holding the money.

What notice ends a monthly tenancy?

Thirty days or more before a monthly period ends, per section 83.57. Year-to-year tenancies need 60 days, quarter-to-quarter 30 days and week-to-week 7 days.

Can I evict a tenant just because I am selling?

Not on that ground alone. You need a legal basis from Chapter 83, such as a properly served nonpayment or violation notice or the end of a periodic tenancy. Check your lease term with a Florida attorney.

How long does the 3-day notice for unpaid rent last?

Three days, not counting Saturdays, Sundays or court-observed legal holidays, under section 83.56(3). It demands payment or possession and can be delivered by mail, hand, e-mail or posting at the home if the tenant is absent.

Who tells the tenant where to send rent after a sale?

The landlord, or the person authorized to receive notices, must tell the tenant in writing who to contact. The authorization stays in place under section 83.50 until the tenant hears otherwise, so a new-owner letter belongs in the closing packet.

We buy as-is, including houses with recorded liens.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

A Florida construction lien does not continue longer than 1 year after the claim of lien is recorded unless suit is filed, and a claim must be recorded within 90 days after the lienor's final furnishing. An owner can shorten the time with a Notice of Contest of Lien.

Selling a house in Florida?
Get My Cash Offer →

What is a mechanic's lien on a Florida home?

It is a claim against the property by someone who supplied labor, services or materials and was not paid. Florida calls it a construction lien, and Chapter 713 of the Florida Statutes sets who can file one and how.

A lien attaches to the real property, not just to the contractor, which is why it shows up in a title search when the owner tries to sell. A lienor who is not in privity with the owner, such as a subcontractor, supplier or sub-subcontractor, can still claim against the home under section 713.06 if the lienor follows the notice steps. The total of all liens for work under one direct contract may not exceed the contract price, with limited exceptions.

What deadlines control a Florida construction lien?

The claim of lien must be recorded no later than 90 days after the lienor's final furnishing of labor, services or materials, under section 713.08(5). It is recorded in the clerk's office, and in each county if the property spans more than one.

A lienor who is not in privity with the owner has an earlier step. Section 713.06(2)(a) requires a notice to owner before starting, or no later than 45 days after starting, to furnish labor, services or materials, and in any event before the owner's final payment after the contractor's affidavit. Failure to serve it, or to serve it on time, is a complete defense to enforcement of the lien. Laborers are excused from that notice.

  • Notice to owner: before starting or within 45 days after starting.
  • Claim of lien recorded: within 90 days after final furnishing.
  • Claim of lien served on the owner: before recording or within 15 days after, or the claim is voidable to the extent the delay prejudiced someone.
  • Suit to enforce: within 1 year of recording the claim.

What must a recorded claim of lien say?

Section 713.08 requires the lienor to state its name and service address, who it contracted with, the labor or materials and their price or value, a legal description, the owner's name, the first and last dates of work, and the amount unpaid.

The claim must be signed and sworn, and it must carry a statutory warning that the lien may remain valid for one year from recording and then expire unless legal proceedings have begun. Errors do not automatically void it. A court can still enforce a lien against someone who was not adversely affected by an omission or mistake, and a claim can be amended while the recording period is still open. Ask a Florida attorney to read the recorded claim against this list, since defects are a common basis for contesting a lien.

How long does the lien last, and how can an owner shorten it?

A lien ends one year after the claim is recorded, unless an action to enforce it has started in court within that time. Section 713.22 sets that period, and a recorded amended claim that shows a later final furnishing date restarts the year.

An owner or the owner's attorney can shorten the time by recording a Notice of Contest of Lien. The lienor then has 60 days from service of the notice to sue, and the lien is extinguished automatically if it does not. The clerk serves the notice on the lienor at the address shown in the claim and records it, and the clerk charges fees for those services.

Even a lien that lives past the year through a filed suit is not enforceable against creditors or later purchasers for value without notice unless a lis pendens is recorded. That detail is part of why title companies check the court docket as well as the property records.

How do you remove a lien so the house can sell?

Section 713.21 lists five ways: a satisfaction entered in the clerk's record, a signed and recorded release, the lienor's failure to sue in time, a court order after a show-cause hearing, or a recorded final judgment.

  1. Pay the lienor and record a notarized satisfaction or release that cites the official records reference number and recording date of the lien.
  2. Wait out the one-year period if no suit was filed, or shorten it with a Notice of Contest.
  3. File a complaint in circuit court. The clerk issues a summons telling the lienor to show cause within 20 days why the lien should not be enforced by action or canceled.
  4. Record a certified judgment showing the final outcome of any enforcement case.

A closing agent can often pay a lien from proceeds if the lienor gives a payoff figure and a release. Recording the release costs clerk fees under section 28.24, starting at $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 for each added page, plus the trust fund and technology charges listed there.

Does a lien come before a mortgage?

Priority depends on recording dates. Under section 713.07, a direct contractor's lien attaches and takes priority as of the time the notice of commencement is recorded, or the claim of lien if no notice was recorded.

Any conveyance, encumbrance or demand recorded before that attach date takes priority over the lien, along with its proceeds regardless of when disbursed. Liens of those not in privity under sections 713.03 and 713.04 attach at recording of the claim. This is why a mortgage recorded before the notice of commencement generally stands ahead, and one recorded afterward may not.

What can a homeowner do to avoid paying twice?

Get written releases each time you pay the contractor, and hold the final payment until the contractor's final payment affidavit arrives. The statutory notice to owner itself warns that unpaid suppliers may lien the property even if the owner paid the contractor in full.

Under section 713.06(3)(d), the contractor must give the owner a sworn affidavit listing any unpaid lienors, and the owner retains the final payment until it is delivered. The contractor must deliver it at least 5 days before suing to enforce a lien. An owner who fails to withhold can remain liable for valid liens of which the owner has notice. For a sale, ask the title company early what it sees on the record.

Frequently asked questions

How long do I have to record a mechanic's lien in Florida?

A lienor must record the claim within 90 days after final furnishing of labor, services or materials, under section 713.08(5). Lienors outside a direct contract with the owner must also serve a notice to owner on time, or the lien can be defeated.

How long does a Florida construction lien last?

One year after the claim is recorded, unless an enforcement suit begins in that time. Section 713.22 also lets an owner record a Notice of Contest that gives the lienor 60 days to sue or lose the lien.

Can I sell my house with a mechanic's lien on it?

Sometimes, but the buyer's title company will want the lien paid, released or otherwise cleared at closing. Ask the lienor for a payoff and a recordable release, or use one of the discharge methods in section 713.21.

Does the lienor have to tell me it filed a lien?

Yes. The claim of lien must be served on the owner. Under section 713.08(4)(c), failing to serve it before recording or within 15 days after makes it voidable to the extent that the delay prejudiced someone.

What is a notice of commencement?

It is the owner's recorded notice for a construction project. Under section 713.07, a direct contractor's lien takes priority as of its recording, or as of the claim of lien if no notice was recorded.

Selling a Florida Condo or HOA Home: Estoppel Certificates and Reserves

Cash Home Buyers in Florida
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Selling a Florida Condo or HOA Home: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Selling a Florida Condo or HOA Home sale
  • Turn the Selling a Florida Condo or HOA Home offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Condo? Get a Cash Offer

We buy condos and HOA homes as-is. Tell us about the building.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

A Florida condominium association must issue an estoppel certificate within 10 business days of a request, and the fee may not exceed $250 if nothing is owed. A buyer is jointly liable with the previous owner for unpaid assessments that came due before transfer.

Selling a house in Florida?
Get My Cash Offer →

What is an estoppel certificate when you sell a Florida condo or HOA home?

An estoppel certificate is the association's written statement of what you owe and what fees apply to your unit or lot as of a given date. The buyer's lender and the title agent rely on it to set the payoff at closing. Condominium associations issue it under section 718.116(8) of the Florida Statutes, and homeowners' associations issue it under section 720.30851.

Request it as soon as you have a signed contract. The association must name on its website a person or entity, with a street or email address, to receive requests, so start there.

How fast must the association deliver it?

Within 10 business days after it receives a written or electronic request from the owner, the owner's designee, or the mortgagee. It must be delivered by hand, regular mail or email on the day it is issued. If the association misses the 10 business days, it cannot charge a fee for that certificate.

A summary court proceeding under section 51.011 can compel compliance, and the winning side recovers reasonable attorney fees. Most sellers never need that, but it shows the weight the statute puts on the deadline.

  • Effective period: 30 days if hand delivered or emailed, 35 days if sent by regular mail.
  • Amended certificate: free of charge if new information or a mistake surfaces in that period, and it starts a new 30 or 35 days.
  • Reliance: the association gives up the right to collect amounts above those stated from anyone who relies on the certificate in good faith.

What can the association charge for it?

The statute caps the fee at $250 when no delinquent amounts are owed on the unit. A request delivered within 3 business days on an expedited basis may add $100. If money is owed to the association, the added fee may not exceed $150. The statute also says the fee authority must come from a written board resolution or a written management contract.

The caps adjust every five years by the Consumer Price Index, and the Department of Business and Professional Regulation publishes the adjusted amounts on its website, so check there before you pay. If the closing falls through and the payer who is not the owner asks within 30 days after the closing date, the fee is refunded within 30 days of the request, and the owner is responsible for the refund.

Estoppel certificate fee limits in section 718.116 and section 720.30851
SituationLimit printed in the statute
No delinquencyReasonable fee, not over $250
Expedited, within 3 business daysAdditional $100
Delinquent amount owedAdditional fee not over $150
Late delivery past 10 business daysNo fee
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What does the certificate have to list?

It lists the regular assessment and how often it is paid, the date it is paid through, and the next installment due. It must include an itemized list of all assessments, special assessments and other money owed, plus items scheduled to come due during the effective period.

Other questions the form asks are useful to a seller before the buyer sees them.

  • Is a capital contribution, resale or transfer fee due, and how much?
  • Is any rule violation open and noticed to the owner?
  • Does the board need to approve the transfer, and has it?
  • Is there a right of first refusal for members or the association, and has it been exercised?
  • Which other associations is the unit a member of, and who insures the association?

The condominium form adds a line for a parking or garage space number and, where the account went to collections, the name and contact information of the attorney, which the association cannot charge for.

Do unpaid assessments follow the unit to the buyer?

Yes, to a degree. Under section 718.116(1), a new unit owner is jointly and severally liable with the previous owner for unpaid assessments that came due before transfer. The new owner may recover from the seller, and the person acquiring title must pay the amount owed to the association within 30 days after the transfer.

Unpaid assessments bear interest at the rate in the declaration, or 18 percent a year if the declaration is silent. If the declaration allows it, the association may add a late fee of up to the greater of $25 or 5 percent of the late installment. Payments go first to interest, then late fees, then collection costs and attorney fees, then the assessment itself.

An association also holds a lien on the condominium parcel. A claim of lien stops being effective one year after recording unless the association starts a suit, and an owner can record a notice of contest that gives the association 90 days to sue. Pay off the figure on the estoppel at closing so the title agent can obtain a lien release.

What must a condo seller hand the buyer?

At the seller's expense, the buyer is entitled to a current copy of the declaration, the articles of incorporation, the bylaws and rules, the annual financial statement and budget, and the Frequently Asked Questions and Answers document. Section 718.503(2) also lists the inspector-prepared summary of any milestone inspection report and the most recent structural integrity reserve study, or a statement that none has been completed.

A resale contract must carry one of two clauses in conspicuous type. One says the buyer got the documents more than 7 days, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays, before signing. The other makes the agreement voidable by written notice within 7 such days after signing and receipt of the documents. A contract that leaves out the required wording can be voided by the buyer before closing.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Why do reserves and structural studies matter to a sale?

A buyer's lender and the buyer will read the budget, and under section 718.112 the budget must include reserve accounts for roof replacement, building painting, pavement resurfacing and any other item whose deferred maintenance or replacement cost exceeds $25,000, or the inflation-adjusted amount published by the division if greater. The amount is computed from estimated remaining useful life and replacement cost.

Residential condominium associations must also complete a structural integrity reserve study at least every 10 years for each building three habitable stories or higher. The statute set a December 31, 2025 deadline for existing associations controlled by owners other than the developer, which has passed. Ask the association whether its study is on file, since the buyer must receive it or a statement that none exists.

The same section lists buildings the study rule does not reach, including those under three stories and one- to four-family dwellings with three or fewer habitable stories. A seller in a low-rise community should check the declaration to see which rules apply.

Frequently asked questions

How long does an association have to issue an estoppel certificate?

Ten business days after a written or electronic request from the owner or the owner's designee, or from the mortgagee. If it is late, the association may not charge for it. Both the condominium and homeowners' association statutes use the same period.

What is the most an association can charge for the certificate?

The cap is $250 when no money is owed, with $100 more for delivery within 3 business days and up to $150 more when an amount is delinquent. The caps adjust every five years, so check the Department of Business and Professional Regulation website for current figures.

How long is an estoppel certificate good for?

Thirty days if hand delivered or sent electronically, and 35 days if mailed. If the sale or refinance has not closed in that window, ask for an amended certificate, which carries no fee and starts a new period.

Do I owe condo assessments after I sell?

You owe the assessments that came due while you owned the unit. The new owner shares liability for unpaid assessments through the transfer date, but the buyer may recover from you, so pay the estoppel balance at closing.

Does a Florida condo seller have to give the buyer a reserve study?

Yes, where one exists. Section 718.503 entitles the buyer to the most recent structural integrity reserve study or a statement that none has been completed, along with the budget and governing documents, at the seller's expense.

Florida Reverse Mortgage: Selling or Inheriting a Home With a HECM

Cash Home Buyers in Florida
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Florida Reverse Mortgage: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Florida Reverse Mortgage sale
  • Turn the Florida Reverse Mortgage offer down and you owe us nothing

Inherited a Home With a Reverse Mortgage? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is and work with the lender and title company.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling a house in Florida?

What happens to a reverse mortgage when the borrower dies?

The loan balance becomes due and payable. HUD's heirs flyer says the loan must be satisfied by the thirtieth day after the borrower dies, and the lender may approve 90-day extensions if the estate or heirs show they are actively trying to sell or repay (HUD, Inheriting a Home Secured by an FHA-insured HECM).

A HECM, or Home Equity Conversion Mortgage, is the reverse mortgage insured by the Federal Housing Administration. While the borrower lives in the house no payments are due, and the balance comes due when the borrower sells, stops using the home as their main home, or dies as the last surviving borrower. HUD adds that no more funds may be paid out once that point is reached.

Those 30 days run out long before most Florida probate cases finish. Call the loan servicer first, ahead of any court filing.

How does a HECM work while the borrower is alive?

HUD describes the HECM as the only reverse mortgage insured by the federal government, available through an FHA-approved lender (HUD HECM page). Borrowers may live in the home indefinitely as long as property taxes and homeowner's insurance stay current.

The amount a borrower can draw depends on three inputs:

  • the age of the youngest borrower or eligible non-borrowing spouse;
  • the current interest rate;
  • the lesser of the appraised value, the FHA mortgage limit or the sales price.

Heirs who are weighing a sale should ask whether the borrower fell behind on taxes or insurance, since that is a common reason servicers call a loan due. HUD points people toward free counseling at (800) 569-4287 and warns against paying scam artists for information that HUD provides at no charge.

What choices do Florida heirs have?

Heirs other than a non-borrowing spouse may repay the loan, sell the home, or hand the property to the lender by a deed in lieu to head off foreclosure. The estate carries property taxes and insurance until title moves.

OptionWhat HUD's flyer says
Sell the homeIf the balance exceeds the home's value, a sale at 95 percent or more of current appraised value lets the lender accept the net proceeds as full payment
Keep the homeThe loan balance must be paid off in full
Deed in lieuTitle goes to the lender to avoid foreclosure
Extension90-day extensions possible with proof of active efforts to sell or repay

Source: HUD flyer dated September 2019. The flyer says any post-death transfer is treated as a "sale" for the 95 percent rule.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What if the borrower's spouse is still living in the house?

A non-borrowing spouse may have extra protection. HUD says special provisions can postpone repayment, allowing the spouse to remain in the property during their lifetime, but the spouse must give the lender a Non-Borrowing Spouse Certification in the first 30 days after the last surviving borrower dies, among other requirements.

That 30-day clock is the one most easily missed during a funeral week. If you are a surviving spouse who was not on the loan, contact the lender and the FHA Resource Center at (800) 225-5342 (listed on the HUD flyer) before any other paperwork.

Whether a particular spouse qualifies depends on conditions that the lender can explain, so ask for them in writing.

What should heirs line up before calling a buyer?

Having the facts in hand lets a buyer, the servicer and the title company work from the same numbers. Gather the following before any offer is accepted:

  • the death certificate and the loan number;
  • the servicer's current payoff figure, which should be requested in writing;
  • proof that taxes and insurance are current, since HUD's flyer leaves those costs with the estate;
  • a current appraisal, because the 95 percent figure is measured against appraised value;
  • the personal representative's name and, where probate is open, a copy of the letters from the court.

If the lender has granted a 90-day extension, keep the paperwork showing active efforts, such as the listing agreement or a signed purchase contract. HUD's flyer ties any extension to that kind of proof, so the file should be ready for the servicer on request.

Heirs who disagree about selling should resolve that early. A servicer's clock keeps running while relatives argue, and only a person with legal authority over the estate can sign a deed.

How does Florida probate affect selling the house?

The house usually sits in the decedent's name, so someone needs legal authority to sign. Florida offers summary administration when the non-exempt estate does not exceed $150,000 or two years have passed since the death (s. 735.201), and formal administration otherwise. Your county probate clerk can say which route fits the house.

Two Florida facts shape the timing:

  • A creditor loses the right to claim unless it files by the later of two dates: 3 months after the notice to creditors is first published, or 30 days after a creditor entitled to direct notice is served (s. 733.702). The reverse mortgage lender is a secured lender, so ask the servicer how it will proceed.
  • Deeds signed by a personal representative under a probated will are on the state's not-taxable list for documentary stamps (DOR page).

Florida levies no estate tax on decedents after 2004, and since July 1, 2023 personal representatives need not file Form DR-312 or DR-313 (DOR estate tax page).

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What if the lender starts foreclosure?

Florida foreclosures go through the courts. After a final judgment the clerk sells the property at public sale not less than 20 days or more than 35 days after judgment unless the plaintiff agrees to a longer period, and the high bidder posts a 5 percent deposit (s. 45.031).

Heirs who want to avoid that path have the hand-the-keys option noted above. Keep every letter from the servicer and answer court papers on time, because a missed deadline limits what you can still do.

A sale before judgment usually leaves the most room. A buyer who closes quickly can pay off the HECM balance at closing, and a buyer taking the house in current condition suits an estate that cannot fund repairs.

Does a reverse mortgage change the property tax picture?

The borrower's homestead benefits depend on the home staying the permanent residence. Homestead is lost, the state says, if the home is rented, stops being the permanent home, or the owner is no longer a Florida permanent resident (DOR homestead guidance).

Once the borrower has died, a sale or transfer of title counts as new ownership, so assessed value resets to just value on the following January 1 unless an exception applies. HUD's flyer reminds heirs that taxes and insurance stay with the estate until title transfers, so budget for them.

To plan your numbers, get a payoff figure from the lender, ask a licensed appraiser for a current value, and ask the county property appraiser how assessments will change.

Frequently asked questions

How long do heirs have to pay off a HECM?

HUD's heirs flyer says the loan must be satisfied in the first 30 days after the borrower's death, and the lender may approve 90-day extensions with documentation of active efforts to sell or repay.

Do heirs owe more than the house is worth?

HUD's flyer says that if the balance exceeds the home's value, heirs may sell for at least 95 percent of the current appraised value and the lender will accept the net proceeds as satisfaction of the loan.

Can heirs keep the house?

Yes, if the HECM balance is paid off in full. HUD says that is the condition for keeping the home.

What can a surviving spouse who was not on the loan do?

HUD says special provisions may allow the spouse to stay for life, but a Non-Borrowing Spouse Certification is due to the lender in the first 30 days after the last borrower's death.

Who pays property taxes on the house after the borrower dies?

HUD's flyer states that property taxes and insurance remain the responsibility of the borrower's estate until title is transferred.
